Grunts should swarm and latch on, draining health until shaken off; each floor ends with a distinct boss pattern before stairs lead upward. Include health, timer, score, lives, floor checkpoints and a final rescue followed by a harder loop.
prompts.watchFor: Generic platformer where contact instantly kills; punch and kick identical; grapplers never latching/draining health; five bosses missing or cloned; no floor timer.

prompts.title: Marble Madness
prompts.prompt: Build Marble Madness as a multi-file web game with mouse/keyboard control and convincing rolling acceleration, momentum and slopes on isometric 3D courses. Race a strict shared timer through six distinct tracks containing ramps, narrow ledges, banked turns, disappearing platforms, catapults, acid, vacuums and enemy marbles. Falling should respawn quickly but cost time; checkpoints prevent full restarts. Support two-player simultaneous racing/collision, remaining-time carryover, score bonuses and a clear finish sequence.
prompts.watchFor: Grid movement; slopes not accelerating the marble; falls costing nothing; flat visuals with no height-aware collision; timer resetting fully each race; no simultaneous versus.

prompts.title: Paperboy
prompts.prompt: Build Paperboy as a multi-file web isometric cycling game across a seven-day route. Steer, accelerate/brake and throw papers left or right with lead timing; deliver to subscribers' mailboxes or porches while avoiding cars, dogs, workers, drains and other moving hazards. Missing deliveries or breaking subscriber windows causes cancellations, while vandalising non-subscriber property earns points. Finish each day on a stunt training course, update the subscriber map, and include lives, score and rising weekday difficulty.
prompts.watchFor: Papers auto-targeting mailboxes; subscriber/non-subscriber houses indistinguishable; missed deliveries not changing the next day's route; obstacles purely cosmetic; no training course.

prompts.title: Punch-Out!!
prompts.prompt: Build Punch-Out!! as a multi-file web boxing game with a transparent over-the-shoulder player view. Provide left/right body blows, left/right head punches, dodge, duck and guard; successful counters build a power meter for a strong uppercut. Create at least four oversized opponents with distinct telegraphs, weak points, guard reactions and phase changes. Use timed three-round bouts, knockdowns and ten-counts, stamina/health recovery between rounds, score, progression and keyboard/gamepad controls.
prompts.watchFor: Side-view button mashing; opponents sharing one AI; attacks lack readable telegraphs/counter windows; head/body targeting identical; no knockdown count or rounds.

prompts.title: Choplifter
prompts.prompt: Build Choplifter as a multi-file web game. Pilot a helicopter with momentum through horizontally scrolling war zones, turn to face left/right or rotate toward the ground, and fire bullets/bombs according to orientation. Land near prison barracks, destroy them to release hostages, wait while survivors board up to the cabin limit, then return and land safely at base. Add tanks, jets and gunboats that threaten both helicopter and people, multiple terrains, hostage quota, fuel/damage, score and lives.
prompts.watchFor: Hostages rescued on touch; no landing/boarding wait; helicopter orientation not affecting fire; enemies unable to kill hostages; unlimited cabin capacity; base return not required.

prompts.title: Commando
prompts.prompt: Build Commando as a multi-file web vertically scrolling run-and-gun game. Move and aim in eight directions while advancing through trenches, bridges and enemy camps. The rifle fires straight along the ground; limited grenades follow an arc over cover and explode after landing, making them mechanically distinct. Add soldiers that rush, fire, throw grenades or use emplacements, rescueable prisoners, authored ambushes, stage-end fortress assaults, score, lives, grenade count and escalating stages.
prompts.watchFor: Grenades as faster bullets; screen auto-clearing without forward progress; enemies spawning randomly with no ambush structure; eight-direction aim missing; no fortress finales.

prompts.title: Gauntlet
prompts.prompt: Build Gauntlet as a multi-file web game for one to four local players. Choose Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard or Elf with distinct speed, armour, melee and ranged strengths. Explore scrolling tile dungeons while health drains continuously; find food, keys, treasure and potions, destroy monster generators before they spawn endless ghosts/grunts/demons, and coordinate through locked doors and exits. Friendly shots can stun allies, food can be contested, and the camera must keep the party together. Include many floors, score and drop-in controls.
prompts.watchFor: Classes differing only by colour; no continuous health drain; generators indestructible or cosmetic; keys/food shared without player interaction; camera allowing party to split infinitely.

prompts.title: Ghosts'n Goblins
prompts.prompt: Build Ghosts'n Goblins as a multi-file web action platformer. Arthur runs, crouches and commits to a fixed mid-air trajectory with a double jump; he throws his equipped weapon and can swap only by picking up a dropped replacement with different range/rate. One hit removes armour and leaves him in underwear, the next kills and returns to a checkpoint. Add zombies rising from terrain, red flying demons, ladders, moving hazards, a strict timer, stage bosses and the false-ending loop requiring the special weapon.
prompts.watchFor: Air steering that erases committed jumps; ordinary health bar instead of armour/underwear states; weapon pickups always upgrades; enemies not spawning from terrain; no checkpoint punishment or second loop.

prompts.title: Hang-On
prompts.prompt: Build Hang-On as a multi-file web pseudo-3D motorcycle racer with projected road segments, hills, curves and depth-scaled rival bikes. Lean into bends, accelerate and brake while choosing lines through traffic; leaving the road slows the bike and hitting scenery or opponents causes a costly crash animation. Reach each checkpoint before time expires as scenery changes across the course. Include speedometer, gear/engine feel, position-independent traffic, lap/checkpoint timing and keyboard/gamepad controls.
prompts.watchFor: Top-down road; steering not expressed as bike lean; no hills/curve projection; crashes reset instantly without lost time; checkpoint timer absent; rivals drawn at fixed size.

prompts.title: Indiana Jones and The Temple of Doom
prompts.prompt: Build Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom as a multi-file web game with three selectable difficulty levels and its repeating three-part structure. In isometric mines, use an aimed whip to fight Thuggee guards, swing gaps and open cages to rescue every child. Then race a mine cart through branching rails, leaning at bends and jumping broken track. Finally infiltrate the temple, recover a Sankara Stone and escape its hazards; after three stones, stage a rope-bridge showdown with Mola Ram. Include score, lives and keyboard/gamepad controls.
prompts.watchFor: Only one of the three gameplay sections; whip as a generic short punch; children freed automatically; mine cart on one safe rail with no jumps/branches; no Stone progression or bridge finale.

prompts.title: Road Runner
prompts.prompt: Build Road Runner as a multi-file web game on scrolling pseudo-isometric roads. Keep ahead of Wile E. Coyote while eating the birdseed placed along the route—missing five seeds makes Road Runner faint and become catchable. Dodge trucks, cliffs, mines, rockets and other traps, but lure Wile E. into his own hazards for bonuses. Add fake iron birdseed and magnets, changing desert layouts, a tease/tongue bonus for letting him approach, score, lives and increasing pursuit speed.
prompts.watchFor: Birdseed as optional score only; Wile E. following a fixed path rather than tracking; his traps unable to backfire; no missed-seed counter/faint state; road never scrolling or changing.

prompts.title: 720º
prompts.prompt: Build 720° as a multi-file web skateboarding game set in Skate City. Use directional momentum, carving and a jump/spin button to chain grinds, airs and rotations while exploring a hub. Spend tickets to enter four events—Downhill, Slalom, Ramp and Jump—earn medals and cash, then buy boards, shoes and pads that materially improve stats. A countdown forces the player to reach the next park; when it expires, a swarm enforces the 'Skate or Die' failure. Include score, upgrades and keyboard/gamepad controls.
prompts.watchFor: Linear event menu with no skateable hub; tricks detached from momentum/rotation; tickets or cash not consumed; equipment cosmetic; timer expiry not producing the pursuing swarm.

prompts.title: Arkanoid
prompts.prompt: Build Arkanoid as a multi-file web game with precise mouse/keyboard paddle control and impact-position ball physics. Arrange many authored brick layouts using ordinary, multi-hit, indestructible and regenerating bricks, plus roaming enemies that deflect the ball. Falling capsules grant mutually managed powers such as wider paddle, catch/release, slow, laser, multi-ball, extra life and a level-exit gate. Include score, lives, increasing ball speed, at least a dozen rounds and a final DOH boss that must be hit repeatedly.
prompts.watchFor: Generic Breakout with no capsules; all brick types identical; catch power not requiring release; multi-ball/lives state breaking; exit capsule auto-clearing without a gate; no boss.

prompts.title: Bubble Bobble
prompts.prompt: Build Bubble Bobble as a multi-file web game with solo and simultaneous two-player co-op. Dragons blow bubbles that trap enemies rather than killing them; pop trapped bubbles by touching/jumping on them to defeat foes and release fruit, with rapid chain pops multiplying rewards. Bubbles drift upward along level-specific airflow and can be bounced on as temporary platforms. Add several enemy behaviours, hurry-up pressure if a stage takes too long, letter bubbles spelling EXTEND, power-ups, score, lives and many compact stages ending in a boss.
prompts.watchFor: Bubbles acting as ordinary lethal bullets; trapped enemies never escaping; no airflow or bubble-platform use; chain scoring absent; co-op and hurry-up pressure missing.

prompts.title: Out Run
prompts.prompt: Build Out Run as a multi-file web pseudo-3D driving game using projected road segments, hills, crests, curves and sprite-scaled traffic/scenery. Drive a fast convertible with low/high gear, throttle, brake and drift-like road handling against checkpoint time. At the end of each stage choose left or right at a visible fork, producing a five-stage route through different scenery and one of several endings. Collisions cause spins or flips with serious time loss. Include selectable music, speedometer, route map and keyboard/gamepad controls.
prompts.watchFor: Top-down racing; road forks cosmetic or always rejoin immediately; no hill/curve projection; traffic not depth-scaled; crashes have no time cost; routes lack distinct endings.

prompts.title: Rampage
prompts.prompt: Build Rampage as a multi-file web game for one to three local players controlling three distinct giant monsters. Climb building faces, move between window ledges, punch individual facade sections and collapse a structure only after enough supports are destroyed. Soldiers, tanks, helicopters and police attack while civilians and food can be grabbed from windows; harmful items reduce health. Players may punch one another, fall from collapsing buildings and revert to a vulnerable human at zero health. Include scrolling cities, score and many days.
prompts.watchFor: Buildings as single health bars; monsters unable to climb/window-hop; military attacks cosmetic; every window item beneficial; no local multiplayer/friendly punching; collapse physics absent.

prompts.title: Rolling Thunder
prompts.prompt: Build Rolling Thunder as a multi-file web side-scrolling spy shooter. Move across upper and lower walkways by jumping up or dropping down, crouch behind low cover to avoid bullets, and enter background doors both to hide and to find marked ammunition/weapon rooms. The pistol has finite bullets; rifle pickups increase power but still require ammo. Masked enemies use colours to signal health/behaviour, emerge from doors and shoot from cover. Include health, timer, stage checkpoints, boss encounters, score and lives.
prompts.watchFor: Unlimited ammunition; doors purely decorative; no upper/lower lane movement or crouch cover; enemy colours cosmetic; player able to absorb many shots without the deliberate pacing.

prompts.title: Super Sprint
prompts.prompt: Build Super Sprint as a multi-file web top-down racer for up to three local players, with AI filling empty cars. Race several laps on compact single-screen circuits using acceleration, braking and momentum-heavy steering. Oil slicks cause spins, water/tornadoes and track edges punish bad lines, and cars can temporarily wreck before a helicopter returns them. Collect wrenches during races and spend sets between rounds on top speed, acceleration or handling upgrades. Include track voting/progression, standings and keyboard/gamepad controls.
prompts.watchFor: Cars snapping to direction with no momentum; upgrades not changing physics; wrecks respawning instantly without helicopter/time loss; no three-player support; hazards only visual.

prompts.title: Wonderboy
prompts.prompt: Build Wonder Boy as a multi-file web side-scrolling platform game. Run and commit to momentum-based jumps while a vitality meter drains constantly; collect fruit to refill it and reach checkpoints before it empties. Find stone axes for ranged attacks, break eggs for upgrades, and ride a skateboard that increases speed and absorbs one hit but makes stopping difficult. Add rocks, fires, moving platforms and enemies, hidden dolls in each area, stage-end boss heads, score, lives and increasingly demanding courses.
prompts.watchFor: Vitality behaving as ordinary hit points instead of time pressure; fruit only adding score; skateboard cosmetic; no egg/axe progression; air control erasing momentum; hidden dolls/bosses absent.

prompts.title: The Secret of Monkey Island
prompts.prompt: Build The Secret of Monkey Island as a multi-file web point-and-click adventure. A SCUMM-style verb grid (Open, Close, Give, Pick up, Look at, Talk to, Use, Push, Pull) sits under the scene next to an inventory panel; clicking a verb and then a hotspot composes a sentence line that resolves, and the sentence must update on hover before the click. Rooms are wider than the viewport and scroll, are connected by exits into a room graph, and each has a walkable floor region the character paths around obstacles within, with depth scaling as they walk upstage. Branching dialogue trees drive the plot. Insult sword-fighting must be a real mechanic, not a cutscene: the player learns insults and retorts by LOSING duels, and each duel is won by matching the correct memorised retort to the opponent's insult. Structure the act as the three trials (treasure, thievery, sword-master) gated by a puzzle dependency graph. The player can never die and can never be permanently stuck — design the state machine so no action can lock the game.
prompts.watchFor: Verb grid decorative — every hotspot resolving to one generic 'use'; no sentence line; walkable region ignored so the sprite walks through scenery or at constant scale; dialogue as a linear cutscene rather than a tree; insult duels resolved by random chance instead of matched retorts; puzzles solvable out of dependency order; any death or dead-end state.

prompts.title: Wing Commander
prompts.prompt: Build Wing Commander as a multi-file web space combat simulator, using three.js for the 3D (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons, so hand-roll the camera and any controls). A cockpit view framed by working instruments: a targeting VDU showing the locked contact and its damage, a radar sphere placing threats around the ship, a damage schematic, and shields split into four quadrants that deplete by hit direction and regenerate over time. Arcade-tuned flight with throttle, afterburner with fuel, pitch/yaw/roll, guns that build heat and cut out, and a limited missile loadout with a lock tone and a lock delay. Fly with a wingman you can order over comms (break and attack, form on my wing, keep formation, return to base) and give the enemy fighters real behaviour: pursuit curves rather than straight lines, breaking off when damaged, taunting over comms, ejecting. Wrap the missions in the campaign layer that made this game matter — a briefing room, a sequence of nav points per mission, a kill board that persists, and a BRANCHING mission tree where a lost mission moves the campaign down the losing series instead of showing a game-over.
prompts.watchFor: Flat 2D dogfighting behind a static cockpit bitmap; shields as a single number instead of four directional quadrants; enemies flying straight at the player with no pursuit curves or break-off; wingman orders that the AI ignores; missiles that always hit with no lock delay; guns with no heat limit; a linear mission list with retry-on-fail instead of a branching win/lose tree; CDN-loaded three.js instead of the vendored copy.

prompts.title: Ultima VI: The False Prophet
prompts.prompt: Build Ultima VI: The False Prophet as a multi-file web tile RPG. The defining feature is ONE seamless map: towns, wilderness and dungeons share a single tile scale with no separate world map and no scale change, so the player walks out of a shop door into open country without a transition screen. Support a party of up to eight, each with their own stats, inventory and equipment, following the leader in single file. Conversation is keyword-driven — the player types or clicks keywords, NPCs always answer NAME and JOB, and highlighted words in their replies become new keywords. NPCs run day/night schedules, walking to work, to the tavern and to bed, and lock up behind them. Objects are real: containers open and nest, items stack, and anything can be picked up, dropped, moved or used, with line-of-sight lighting in dungeons and after dark. Turn-based combat plays out on the same map the player explores, never a separate arena screen. Include moongates on a lunar cycle, a karma system that tracks theft and murder, and the gargoyle plot in which the monsters turn out to have their own side of the story.
prompts.watchFor: Separate overworld and town maps with a scale change; party members as passive stat blocks that take no combat turns; a fixed dialogue menu instead of keyword parsing with discoverable keywords; NPCs standing still with no schedules; combat cutting away to a separate arena screen; scenery painted into the background rather than being real, movable objects; no line-of-sight or lighting; karma that never changes.

prompts.title: King's Quest V: Absence Makes the Heart Go Yonder!
prompts.prompt: Build King's Quest V as a multi-file web graphical adventure. This was Sierra's first ICON-driven game, so there must be no text parser anywhere: a top icon bar (walk, look, hand, talk, taste, inventory, and a help cursor) where the selected icon becomes the mouse cursor and clicking a hotspot applies that specific action, with distinct responses per icon per hotspot. Painted screens connect as a room graph with edge transitions, and every room needs a walkable-area mask plus walk-behind regions with per-column depth so Graham passes correctly in front of and behind scenery and scales as he moves. Inventory items can be selected as the cursor and used on the world, and an item can be inspected close-up. Keep the era-authentic stakes rather than smoothing them away: the player CAN die, with a death screen offering restore, restart or quit, and the player CAN make the game unwinnable by consuming, losing or failing to collect a needed item. Track winnability explicitly in state and surface it — do not silently prevent it. Ship a working save/restore with multiple slots, because the design depends on it.
prompts.watchFor: A text parser bolted on alongside the icons; every icon producing the same generic response; no walk-behind or depth scaling so the sprite draws over all scenery at one size; death handled as an instant respawn with no restore/restart prompt; items not actually consumed, making the unwinnable state unreachable; winnability not tracked; no save/restore, or a single autosave slot.

prompts.title: Loom
prompts.prompt: Build Loom as a multi-file web adventure with NO inventory and NO verb list — the whole interface is a distaff that plays four-note melodies. Map eight tones (C D E F G A B C) onto the distaff, playable by mouse and by keyboard, each with a real pitch through Web Audio (or Tone.js, vendored) and a matching colour and staff position. Every spell is a four-note 'draft' that the player must first HEAR somewhere in the world — a swan's call, a spinning wheel, a shepherd's flock, a dying man — and then play back at the right target. Reversing a draft's notes inverts its effect, so Dye becomes Unedye and Open becomes Close: this must fall out of the note logic itself, not be special-cased per spell. Audio is the mechanic, so the world must sing drafts at the player and the player answers by ear. Include the original's difficulty settings: Practice draws the note names on the staff as you play, Standard draws the staff only, Expert shows nothing at all. Add scrolling painted rooms, a draft book that fills itself in as drafts are learned, and story gates that open on which drafts the player actually knows.
prompts.watchFor: Drafts chosen from a menu or spell list instead of played note by note on the distaff; notes silent, or all the same pitch, or with no visual feedback; reversal hard-coded per spell rather than derived from playing the notes backwards; an inventory or verb bar creeping back in; the draft book pre-filled at the start; a single difficulty with the notes always labelled; story gates opened by scene counter rather than by known drafts.

prompts.title: Sid Meier's Civilization
prompts.prompt: Build Sid Meier's Civilization as a multi-file web turn-based strategy game. Open in 4000 BC with a single settler on a procedurally generated world map of real terrain types (grassland, plains, hills, mountains, forest, desert, swamp, tundra, ocean), each with its own food, production and trade yields and its own movement cost, hidden under fog of war that units reveal as they explore. Settlers found cities; a city works the tiles in its radius, grows on surplus food, turns production into units and buildings, and slides into civil disorder if too many citizens are unhappy. Research is funded by accumulated trade and spends down a TECH TREE with real prerequisites, where each discovery unlocks units, buildings and forms of government from Despotism through Monarchy to Republic and Democracy, and each government trades production and martial law against corruption and war weariness. Rival AI civilizations must genuinely play the same game: expand, found cities, research, declare war, and open diplomacy with demands, tribute and peace treaties. Resolve combat from attack and defence strength modified by terrain, fortification and veteran status, not by a coin flip. Add Wonders of the World as once-per-game builds with unique global effects, and finish the game by conquest, by the space race to Alpha Centauri, or on the time limit with a scored ranking of every civilization.
prompts.watchFor: A uniform map, or terrain that changes neither yields nor movement cost; no fog of war; cities as a build menu with no worked tiles, food growth or unhappiness; a linear upgrade list instead of a branching tech tree with prerequisites; governments that are cosmetic labels; AI civs that never expand, research or declare war; combat as a pure coin flip with no terrain or fortification modifiers; only one victory condition; wonders that are just expensive buildings.

prompts.title: Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge
prompts.prompt: Build Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge as a multi-file web point-and-click adventure in the refined SCUMM style: a verb grid, an inventory drawn as ICONS rather than a text list, and a sentence line that composes on hover before the click commits. The technical headline is iMUSE-style ADAPTIVE MUSIC and it is the requirement that must not be dropped — every room has a theme, and walking between rooms or entering a conversation must never cut the track dead; the score transitions on the next beat or bar and layers instruments in and out as the scene changes, so the music follows the player continuously. Structure it as four acts: Largo LaGrande's grip on Scabb Island, then a three-island hub of Scabb, Phatt and Booty that the player sails between freely, framed throughout by Guybrush narrating the story to someone. Because the islands are open at once, the puzzle dependency graph must genuinely span them — items found on one island solve problems on another — rather than gating one room at a time. Dialogue trees carry the comedy and must branch on what the player has already seen. Offer the original's two difficulty modes: the full game, and a cut-down 'Lite' version that removes entire puzzle chains rather than just adding hints. Nobody can die and nothing can be made unwinnable.
prompts.watchFor: Music restarting from zero or cutting dead on every room change instead of transitioning on a beat; inventory rendered as a text list; no sentence line; a single-island linear puzzle chain with no cross-island dependencies; dialogue collapsed into one-shot cutscenes that ignore prior state; boat travel that is a menu rather than a hub; Lite mode identical to the full game; any death or dead-end state.

prompts.title: Duke Nukem
prompts.prompt: Build the original 1991 Duke Nukem as a multi-file web 2D action platformer. Tile-based levels far larger than the viewport that scroll smoothly in every direction, with Duke running, jumping and shooting horizontally, and a jetpack pickup with a draining fuel gauge that opens the level up vertically. The scenery must be INTERACTIVE rather than decoration, which is the whole texture of the game: crates and barrels break apart into pickups, monitors, cameras, lights and signs can be shot for points, wall switches drop force fields and open doors, and coloured keycards gate whole sections of the map. Give Duke a weapon that upgrades through tiers and persists between levels, a health bar rather than one-hit death, extra lives, and a score with hidden bonus items rewarding players who search. Enemies need distinct behaviour, not one shared pattern — patrolling ground troops, fixed turrets that lead their shots, flying drones that dive — and each level ends properly, with the episode closing on a multi-phase Dr. Proton boss fight that changes attack pattern as its health drops. Structure the whole thing as episodic shareware: three episodes of several levels, only the first playable, ending on a screen that sells the other two.
prompts.watchFor: A single screen-sized level with no scrolling, or scrolling on one axis only; scenery as painted background that cannot be shot or broken; no keycards or switches, so the map is a straight corridor; a weapon that never upgrades, or that resets every level; one-hit death instead of a health bar; enemies sharing one movement and fire pattern; the boss as a bullet sponge with no phase changes; no episode structure or end-of-episode gate.

prompts.title: Another World (Out of This World)
prompts.prompt: Build Another World (Out of This World) as a multi-file web cinematic platformer. Render EVERYTHING as filled and outlined polygons — no sprite sheets, no bitmaps, no tile art anywhere: Lester, the aliens, the beasts, the scenery and the cutscenes all come out of the same polygon list, drawn into a low-resolution buffer and scaled up, because that single decision is what gives the game its look. Animate Lester from rotoscoped keyframes so running, jumping, crouching, rolling and climbing carry weight and momentum, with wind-up and follow-through on every action instead of instant response. There is NO HUD, NO score, NO health bar and NO readable text or dialogue — the story must be carried entirely by staging, camera framing and animation, and cutscenes must run through the same polygon renderer as gameplay so the cuts between them are seamless. Death is instant and frequent by design; make that fair with a checkpoint at the start of every set-piece so a retry is immediate. Arm the player with a plasma gun whose three functions all come from how long the fire button is held: a quick shot, a deployed energy shield that blocks incoming fire, and a slow charged blast that breaks shields and walls. Include the alien companion, and give him real initiative — he must go off and solve things the player cannot reach and wait to be caught up with, never trail behind as a shadow. Puzzles are physical set-pieces: levers, cages, rising water, collapsing floors, a stampeding beast.
prompts.watchFor: Sprite sheets or tile art instead of polygon rendering; instant-response movement with no animation wind-up or momentum; a HUD, health bar, score or readable dialogue appearing anywhere; cutscenes as image sequences or video rather than the same renderer; checkpoints so far apart that instant death becomes unfair; a gun with one fire mode and no held-button shield or charged blast; the companion following as a mirror with no independent actions of his own.

prompts.title: Wolfenstein 3D
prompts.prompt: Build Wolfenstein 3D as a multi-file web first-person shooter, and implement the RAYCASTER yourself against a 2D canvas — no three.js, no WebGL engine, no 3D library, because hand-rolling the renderer is the whole exercise. Cast one ray per screen column across a grid of wall tiles, take the perpendicular distance to kill the fisheye effect, derive each column's height and texture coordinate from that hit, and draw textured wall strips with a light/dark shade per wall face. Everything that is not a wall is a billboard sprite — enemies, lamps, pickups, decorations — depth-sorted and scaled against the same per-column depth buffer so they clip correctly behind walls. Levels are 64x64 tile mazes with push-wall secret doors, sliding doors that open on use, and coloured keycards. Give the player a weapon wheel of knife, pistol, machine gun and chaingun, sharing one ammo pool, and enemies (guards, SS, dogs) that patrol on waypoints, react to gunfire noise in nearby rooms, shout when they spot you, and fire with distance-based accuracy. Fill the HUD with the era-correct panel: face portrait that reacts to health, health, ammo, score, lives, keys and floor number. End each floor at a lift switch, and finish the episode on a boss with a scripted arena.
prompts.watchFor: Using three.js or WebGL instead of writing the raycaster; fisheye distortion left uncorrected by not using perpendicular distance; walls untextured or flat-shaded with no per-face light/dark; sprites not depth-tested against the column buffer so they draw over walls; enemies unaware of gunshots and standing still until seen; no push-wall secrets or keycard doors; a HUD missing the reactive face portrait; every weapon behaving identically.

prompts.title: Dune II: The Battle for Arrakis
prompts.prompt: Build Dune II: The Battle for Arrakis as a multi-file web real-time strategy game — the game that set the template, so the template has to be there in full. The economy is spice: harvesters drive out to spice fields, fill up, drive back to a refinery and unload into credits, and credits are the only thing that pays for construction, which means a harvester lost is an economy stalled. Sandworms roam the open sand and swallow units that linger. Building works through a construction yard: you buy a structure from a sidebar list, then place it on the map, and it must be placed adjacent to existing buildings on prepared concrete, or it takes damage from the sand. Structures unlock further structures and units in a per-house tech progression, and power plants must keep up with demand or everything runs degraded. Give the three houses genuinely different rosters — Atreides, Ordos and Harkonnen, each with a unique unit and its own feel. Units need real orders (move, attack, guard, harvest, repair), turrets need firing arcs, and the enemy AI must build its own base, expand its economy and mount attack waves rather than spawning units from nowhere. Wrap it in the campaign: a map of Arrakis where the player picks the next territory to attack, with a mentat briefing before each mission and fog of war over unexplored ground.
prompts.watchFor: Spice as an abstract trickle of income instead of harvesters physically hauling it to a refinery; no sandworms; buildings placeable anywhere with no concrete or adjacency rule; a flat build list with no structure-unlocks-structure tech progression; power ignored; the three houses identical apart from colour; enemy units spawning out of thin air instead of being built in a real base; AI that never expands or attacks in waves; no fog of war; a fixed mission order with no territory choice.

prompts.title: Ultima VII: The Black Gate
prompts.prompt: Build Ultima VII: The Black Gate as a multi-file web open-world RPG. What separates this from every other RPG of its era is that the world is an OBJECT SIMULATION, not scenery, and that is the requirement to protect: every item is a real object with real properties and real uses, containers nest inside containers, and the player interacts by dragging things with the mouse rather than by picking verbs from a menu. It must be possible to take flour and water, make dough, put it in an oven and bake bread; to pick up every plate, fork and candle in a house and stack them somewhere else; to work a loom, a grinding wheel, a forge. Movement and combat are REAL-TIME, not turn-based — the party fights on its own under a chosen combat stance while the player acts, which is the break from Ultima VI. Support a party that follows the leader, each member with equipment, inventory and their own opinions in conversation. NPCs live on full day/night schedules, unlock and lock their shops, eat at the tavern and sleep at home, and conversation runs on branching topic keywords rather than a fixed menu. Layer the Fellowship plot over the top: a wholesome-sounding organisation the player is invited to join, whose members can be followed, questioned and caught out, so the investigation is played rather than narrated.
prompts.watchFor: Items as inventory strings rather than real world objects; containers that cannot nest; a verb menu instead of drag-and-drop interaction; no multi-step crafting (the flour to bread chain is the acceptance test); turn-based combat, which is Ultima VI's model and the thing this game replaced; party members that stand still while the leader fights; NPCs without schedules; menu dialogue with no keyword branching; the Fellowship reduced to a plot summary the player cannot investigate.

prompts.title: Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis
prompts.prompt: Build Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis as a multi-file web point-and-click adventure in the SCUMM style — verb grid, icon inventory, sentence line on hover. The headline feature, and the reason the game is replayable, is the THREE PATHS: after a shared opening the player is offered the Team path (travel with Sophia, who solves problems through conversation and argument), the Wits path (solo, the hardest, built on lateral puzzles) and the Fists path (action-led, resolved with brawling). These must be three genuinely different routes through the middle of the game with different locations, different puzzles and different solutions to the same obstacles, converging again for the finale — not one route with cosmetic reskins. Model Sophia as a real companion on the Team path: she can be talked to about any object or topic, comments on scenes, and is required to solve certain puzzles. Include the fist-fighting as a simple timing-and-blocking exchange rather than a reflex test, and always leave a non-combat way past when the path allows it. Travel between real locations — New York, the Azores, Algiers, Crete, Thera — through a map screen. Track an IQ (Indy Quotient) score that accumulates per puzzle solved and persists between playthroughs, so replaying a different path is rewarded, and show which of the three routes each point came from.
prompts.watchFor: The three paths sharing one puzzle chain with only dialogue changes; the path choice offered but never actually branching the map; Sophia as a silent follower with no conversation or puzzle role; fist fights as unwinnable filler or as the only way past an obstacle on every path; no travel map; IQ score reset each playthrough or not tracked per path; any death or unwinnable state.

prompts.title: Alone in the Dark
prompts.prompt: Build Alone in the Dark as a multi-file web survival horror game using three.js for the actors (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons, so hand-roll the camera work). The defining technique is the hybrid: real-time POLYGONAL 3D characters and creatures composited over hand-drawn, pre-rendered 2D backgrounds, with a FIXED camera per room that cuts to a new angle as the player crosses a threshold. Render the backdrop as a full-screen image, place the polygon actors in a 3D scene aligned to that image's camera, and drive collision from an invisible per-room geometry that matches the drawing — so the player walks behind furniture and is occluded by it correctly. Controls are relative to the character, not the screen, so a camera cut does not reverse the player's direction mid-step. Let the player choose Edward Carnby or Emily Hartwood, with different starting items. Build the mansion as a connected set of rooms with a real inventory: keys, a lamp, weapons with scarce ammunition, and consumable items. Crucially, this is horror and not an action game — several creatures CANNOT be killed and must be escaped, blocked with furniture that the player physically pushes, or avoided entirely, and the player must find that out the hard way. Scatter books, diaries and letters that are readable in full and that contain the actual solutions to those encounters, so reading is a mechanic and not flavour text.
prompts.watchFor: A fully 3D room instead of polygon actors over a pre-rendered backdrop; a free or following camera instead of fixed per-room angles; screen-relative controls that reverse the player on a camera cut; actors drawing over furniture because there is no occlusion geometry; every monster killable, which removes the horror; ammo unlimited; books and letters as unreadable props or as flavour with no solutions in them; only one playable character; CDN-loaded three.js instead of the vendored copy.

prompts.title: Doom (Web)
prompts.prompt: Build Doom as a multi-file web first-person shooter, and write the renderer yourself against a 2D canvas — no three.js, no WebGL engine, and specifically NOT a raycaster, because a raycaster is Wolfenstein's technique and what made Doom different is the SECTOR renderer. Model the level as sectors: closed polygons of walls at arbitrary angles, each sector carrying its own independent floor height, ceiling height and light level, connected through portal linedefs. Sort them front-to-back with a BSP tree, draw textured wall, floor and ceiling spans, and darken by distance so corridors fade out. Because floors have height, the level must work vertically: stairs, ledges, lifts that rise and fall, doors that open on use or on a trigger, crushing ceilings, damaging slime floors, and light levels that flicker or pulse per sector. Enemies are billboard sprites with eight rotation frames so you can see which way they face, and they need real behaviour — patrol, wake on noise, chase through doorways, and INFIGHT: when one monster's attack hits another, they must turn on each other, which is the acceptance test that damage is properly attributed. Give hitscan weapons (pistol, shotgun, chaingun) and projectile weapons (rockets with splash damage, plasma) sharing distinct ammo pools. Add coloured keycards, secret areas found by pushing walls, a rotating automap, and network deathmatch and co-op for at least two players.
prompts.watchFor: A raycaster on a uniform grid instead of a sector renderer, which caps every room at one floor height; walls locked to 90-degree angles; floors and ceilings untextured flat colour; no distance-based light falloff or per-sector light levels; no lifts, stairs or crushers, so the level is functionally flat; enemies as single-facing sprites; no monster infighting, meaning damage is not attributed to its source; splash damage missing from rockets; no automap; no multiplayer at all.

prompts.title: Myst
prompts.prompt: Build Myst as a multi-file web first-person puzzle adventure. Navigation is NODE-BASED and that constraint is the whole atmosphere: the player stands at a discrete viewpoint, clicks a hotspot in the frame, and the view transitions to another fixed viewpoint. There is no free-roaming camera, no walking, no strafing. Use three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons) to build each Age as real geometry and render the node views from it, so the world can be authored geometrically instead of requiring hand-painted art, but keep the camera pinned to the node graph and animate the cut between nodes. There is no inventory, no HUD, no health, no combat, no dialogue tree, no timer and no way to die or to lose. Every puzzle must be a MACHINE whose logic is observable in the world — a rotating tower that aims at things, a clock with gears, a spaceship organ that plays tones, a mine cart with a direction switch — solvable purely by looking, listening and deducing, never by being told the answer. Start on Myst Island, put linking books in the library that carry the player to four distinct Ages, and make the Ages independently solvable in any order. Scatter journals that can be read page by page and that hold the real information. Close it on the two brothers, their red and blue book pages, and a genuine choice with several different endings.
prompts.watchFor: Free WASD movement instead of node-to-node clicking; an inventory or HUD appearing; any death, fail state or timer; puzzles whose solution is spelled out in a text popup rather than deducible from observing the machine; the four Ages gated into a fixed linear order; journals as one-screen summaries rather than readable page by page; a single ending; CDN-loaded three.js instead of the vendored copy.

prompts.title: Day of the Tentacle
prompts.prompt: Build Day of the Tentacle as a multi-file web point-and-click adventure in cartoon SCUMM style — verb grid, icon inventory, sentence line. Three playable characters are stranded in the SAME mansion in three different centuries: Bernard in the present, Hoagie two hundred years in the past, Laverne two hundred years in the future. The player switches between them freely at any time, and each era is a full explorable version of the mansion whose rooms mirror each other but have aged. Items move between eras through the Chron-o-John, so one character's inventory can be flushed to another. The thing that must be built properly, and the reason this game is remembered, is CAUSALITY as real propagated state and not as scripted cutscenes: an action taken in the past has to modify the world model, and the present and future must then read that modified model. The acceptance test is a chain like leaving an object in the past and finding its aged, transformed or relocated consequence centuries later — change the past again and the later eras must change again. Build the puzzle dependency graph explicitly across all three eras so the majority of puzzles require at least two characters cooperating across time. Nobody can die and nothing can become unwinnable, and dialogue trees carry the comedy.
prompts.watchFor: Eras as three separate levels with no shared world state; past actions handled by playing a fixed cutscene in the future rather than by propagating state; a per-character inventory that cannot be transferred between eras; puzzles solvable by one character alone in one era, making the time travel decorative; the character switch as a level select with progress lost; any death or dead-end state; a text-list inventory or a missing sentence line.

prompts.title: SimCity 2000
prompts.prompt: Build SimCity 2000 as a multi-file web city-building simulation. Render it in an ISOMETRIC projection you compute yourself over a terrain heightmap, because elevation is the leap this game made: land has height, the player can raise, lower and level terrain before building, water sits at a sea level, and slopes constrain what can be placed. Add the UNDERGROUND view as a separate toggled layer holding water pipes and subway tunnels, so the city exists on two levels. Drive growth from RCI demand meters against zoned residential, commercial and industrial land. Make the utilities real systems rather than decoration: a power grid where connectivity is actually traced from plant to zone, so an unwired zone stays dark and dies, and plants that expire after a fixed lifetime; a water system with pumps that must sit near fresh water and pipes that must reach each tile. Add roads, rails and highways with on-ramps, and let traffic congest. Give the player a budget with a tax rate per zone type and per-department funding sliders for police, fire, transit, education and health, where underfunding visibly degrades the city, plus city ordinances with running costs. Include disasters that spread and must be fought — fire, flood, tornado, earthquake, air crash, monster. Provide a query tool that reports per-tile land value, pollution, crime and traffic, a newspaper reporting on events, and arcologies as the late game.
prompts.watchFor: A flat grid with no terrain elevation or land grading; no underground layer; power delivered by proximity instead of a traced grid, so wires are cosmetic; power plants that never expire; water system absent; RCI demand as a fixed growth timer rather than a simulation; funding sliders that change nothing; disasters as instant tile deletion rather than something that spreads and can be fought; no per-tile query for land value, crime and pollution.

prompts.title: Syndicate
prompts.prompt: Build Syndicate as a multi-file web real-time tactical game, isometric, dark and neon, over a rain-lit cyberpunk city. The player fields a squad of four cyborg agents, selectable individually or as a group, moving and shooting in real time on dense city maps full of civilians who panic and flee, police who respond to gunfire, and cars that can be commandeered and driven. The signature weapon is the PERSUADERTRON: aim it at a civilian, a policeman or even an enemy agent and they are converted, joining the squad as a following entourage that fights alongside it, with the number you can hold growing as you persuade more. Give each agent three chemical sliders — Adrenaline, Perception and Intelligence — that trade speed, accuracy and reaction time against a finite supply that drains while boosted and leaves the agent sluggish when spent. Between missions, run the syndicate itself: fit cybernetic upgrades to each agent's legs, arms, chest, heart, eyes and brain from mission earnings; fund a research lab that develops weapons and modifications over elapsed time rather than instantly; and take territories on a world map, where each conquered territory pays tax at a rate the player sets and revolts if taxed too hard. Missions must go beyond kill-everyone: assassinate a named target, persuade a specific scientist, steal an item, or wipe out a rival squad.
prompts.watchFor: Turn-based movement instead of real time; agents controllable only as one blob with no individual orders; no Persuadertron, or persuaded people that follow without fighting; the drug sliders as free permanent buffs with no finite supply or comedown; research completing instantly; a linear mission list with no world map, territories or tax rate; civilians and police as static scenery; every mission being kill-everything; no vehicles.

prompts.title: X-COM: UFO Defense
prompts.prompt: Build X-COM: UFO Defense as a multi-file web game, and build BOTH layers, because the whole design is the loop between them. The Geoscape is a rotating globe running in real time with pause and time acceleration: UFOs appear and fly missions, radar at your bases detects them, interceptors scramble and fight them in a short air-combat exchange, and downed craft leave crash sites. On that layer you build and lay out bases room by room, hire and fire soldiers, scientists and engineers, run a RESEARCH tree that is gated by recovered material — you cannot research alien plasma weapons until you have recovered one, and cannot finish the interrogation line until you have captured a LIVE alien — manufacture equipment to use or sell, and answer to funding nations whose monthly funding rises or falls on your performance and who defect to the aliens if you fail them. The Battlescape is turn-based squad tactics on a destructible isometric grid: every soldier has TIME UNITS spent on moving, turning, firing and reloading, aimed/snap/auto shots costing different amounts, line of sight and darkness limiting what you see, and REACTION FIRE letting a soldier who saved Time Units interrupt the enemy's turn. Soldiers carry an inventory laid out by slot, improve their stats through use, and die permanently. Include terror missions in cities, assaults on landed UFOs, and alien attacks on your own base.
prompts.watchFor: Only one of the two layers built; Geoscape as a mission menu rather than a live globe with detection and interception; research available immediately instead of gated on recovered artefacts and live captives; funding nations that never react or withdraw; Battlescape using movement points that ignore turning, firing and reloading rather than true Time Units; no reaction fire, which removes the whole risk model; terrain that is not destructible; no line of sight or darkness; soldiers respawning instead of dying permanently; no base building or base defence.

prompts.title: System Shock
prompts.prompt: Build System Shock as a multi-file web immersive sim using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons, so hand-roll the controls and camera). Set it aboard Citadel Station, a connected multi-level space station the player explores and backtracks through, not a corridor of levels. Movement must have the full freedom that separated this from its contemporaries: free look up and down, lean left and right around corners, crouch and go prone to fit through ducts, jump and climb ladders, with real vertical level geometry rather than a flat floor plan. There are no conversations and no NPCs — the ENTIRE story is told through audio logs and emails the player finds and can replay from a log screen, so the narrative must be discoverable, missable and re-readable. SHODAN is the antagonist and must feel present: she watches the player over cameras that can be destroyed, taunts them on triggered events, and locks or alters parts of the station in response to what they do. Give the player hardware implants that each add an overlay to the HUD — targeting, night vision, motion sensor, data reader — and each drain a shared power budget so they cannot all run at once. Build a real inventory with weapon mods, and several ammo types whose effectiveness differs sharply between mutants, robots and cyborgs. Add a wireframe CYBERSPACE mode with different physics for hacking, and cyborg conversion chambers that respawn the player until they are found and disabled on each level.
prompts.watchFor: Doom-style movement with no look up/down, lean, crouch or prone; a flat single-height floor plan with no real verticality; story delivered by cutscene or an NPC talking instead of found audio logs; logs that cannot be replayed; SHODAN as a static end boss with no presence during play; implants as permanent free buffs with no power drain or trade-off; one universal ammo type; no cyberspace sections; respawn handled as a checkpoint rather than the in-world conversion chambers; CDN-loaded three.js instead of the vendored copy.

prompts.title: DOOM II: Hell on Earth
prompts.prompt: Build DOOM II: Hell on Earth as a multi-file web first-person shooter with a hand-written SECTOR renderer on a 2D canvas — BSP-sorted sectors with independent floor and ceiling heights, portals, texture-mapped walls, floors and ceilings, and distance light falloff. No raycaster and no three.js. Then build what actually makes this the sequel rather than the original. The SUPER SHOTGUN is the centrepiece: a double-barrelled weapon firing a wide 20-pellet spread with a long, committed reload, devastating up close and useless at range, and it must change how the player fights. Ship the new bestiary and give each monster a mechanic rather than more health: the Arch-vile, which sets the player alight from across the room and RESURRECTS other monsters' corpses, so leaving bodies lying around has consequences; the Pain Elemental, which spawns Lost Souls continuously until killed; the Revenant, with homing rockets that must be dodged around corners; the Mancubus with wide flame spreads; the Arachnotron; the Hell Knight; and the Chaingunner who shreds the player at range. Replace the episode structure with one continuous thirty-level campaign that moves from ruined Earth cities to Hell, with larger, more open architecture than corridor crawling. Keep monster infighting working, since the Arch-vile makes it matter more. Finish on the Icon of Sin: a wall-sized demon that endlessly spawns monsters and can only be killed by rocketing its exposed brain. Include deathmatch and co-op.
prompts.watchFor: A raycaster or three.js instead of a hand-written sector renderer; the Super Shotgun as a reskinned shotgun with no spread or reload commitment; the Arch-vile not resurrecting corpses, which is its entire point; Pain Elementals that do not spawn Lost Souls; Revenant rockets that fly straight instead of homing; new monsters differing only in hit points; an episode structure instead of one continuous campaign; corridor-only level geometry; no monster infighting; the Icon of Sin as an ordinary health-bar boss rather than a spawner with an exposed weak point; no multiplayer.

prompts.title: Warcraft: Orcs & Humans
prompts.prompt: Build Warcraft: Orcs & Humans as a multi-file web real-time strategy game. Two resources, not one, and they behave differently: peasants and peons mine GOLD from a gold mine with a finite deposit that runs dry, and chop LUMBER from forest tiles that are actually REMOVED from the map as they are felled, so terrain changes permanently as the economy runs. Buildings are placed freely on buildable ground rather than on prepared foundations, and a farm-style food supply caps how many units can exist, forcing expansion. Give both sides a full campaign with mirrored but distinctly flavoured rosters — footman against grunt, archer against spearman, catapult against catapult — and real spellcasters with a mana pool and separate spell lists: conjurer and cleric for the humans, warlock and necrolyte for the orcs, with summons, healing, invisibility and raise-dead as distinct tactical tools rather than damage in different colours. Support selecting and ordering a small group of units at once, unit stances and orders (move, attack, patrol, harvest, repair, build), and roads. The enemy AI must build a real base, gather its own resources and send attack waves, never spawn units from nothing. Include the on-foot dungeon-style missions where a handful of units explore a passage map with no base at all, and build head-to-head multiplayer for two players, which is what set this apart from its predecessors.
prompts.watchFor: A single resource; forests that are decorative and never actually cleared by lumber harvesting; gold mines with infinite deposits; no food or supply cap; the two factions identical apart from sprite colour; spellcasters with no mana or with spells that are just recoloured damage; single-unit selection only; enemy units spawning from thin air instead of being built in a base that gathers resources; no dungeon missions; no multiplayer.

prompts.title: Theme Park
prompts.prompt: Build Theme Park as a multi-file web business management simulation, isometric and bright. The player lays out paths, rides, shops and scenery in a park, and GUESTS ARE INDIVIDUAL AGENTS, which is the requirement everything else hangs off: each guest walks the paths you actually built, and carries happiness, hunger, thirst, tiredness, bladder and cash that all change over time and drive what they do next. Bad path layout must genuinely lose you guests — they get lost, get tired, get angry and leave — and queues must form as real lines at ride entrances. Model the shops the way the original gleefully did: per-item recipe sliders where over-salting the fries makes guests thirsty and sells more drinks, and watering down the drinks raises margin but tanks satisfaction, with prices set per item. Hire staff with wages and let them be underpaid: handymen sweep litter and empty bins, mechanics service rides, entertainers cheer queues, security stop vandals and pickpockets, and if wages fall behind the staff go on STRIKE and stop working. Ride safety must degrade with use so an unmaintained ride eventually crashes. Add a research budget that unlocks new rides and shops over time, negotiation with suppliers over stock prices, and a world map where parks in different countries have different costs, tastes and land prices, with a share price and the option to buy and sell parks.
prompts.watchFor: Guests as an abstract visitor counter instead of individual pathing agents; guests teleporting to rides rather than walking the built paths; no queues; needs like thirst and bladder tracked but never affecting behaviour; shop recipe sliders absent or with no effect on thirst and satisfaction; staff as a flat upkeep cost with no strikes and no actual sweeping or repairing; rides that never degrade or crash; research instant; a single park with no world map, land prices or share price.

prompts.title: Command & Conquer
prompts.prompt: Build Command & Conquer as a multi-file web real-time strategy game. Harvesters drive out to Tiberium fields, fill up and return to a refinery, and the field is physically consumed as they mine, so the map's economy visibly depletes. Construction runs through a SIDEBAR: you queue a building, it charges you progressively as it builds, and when ready you get a placement cursor that must go on cleared ground near your existing base. Base power matters as a global budget — fall short and radar dies, superweapons stall and production slows. Give GDI and Nod genuinely asymmetric rosters rather than reskins: GDI heavy and direct with mammoth tanks, orcas and the Ion Cannon; Nod fast, cheap and dirty with stealth tanks that decloak only to fire, flame throwers, obelisks of light and the nuclear strike. Both superweapons run on long cooldown timers and must be charged. Add box drag-selection of multiple units, engineers that capture an enemy building outright by walking into it, commandos that one-shot infantry and demolish structures, unit orders (move, attack, force-fire, guard), and fog of war. The enemy AI must build a real base, harvest its own Tiberium and stage attack waves.
prompts.watchFor: Tiberium as an income trickle instead of a physically depleted field; buildings placeable anywhere with no base adjacency; power ignored, so radar and superweapons always work; GDI and Nod identical apart from colour; stealth units permanently visible or permanently invisible; superweapons on no cooldown; engineers that damage buildings rather than capturing them; enemy units spawning instead of being produced from a working base.

prompts.title: Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness
prompts.prompt: Build Warcraft II: Tides of Darkness as a multi-file web real-time strategy game. It takes the first game's gold and lumber and adds the thing that reshaped it: the SEA. Oil is a third resource pumped by tankers from offshore oil patches and hauled to a refinery, and it pays for the entire naval and air tier — so maps with water play completely differently from land maps. Build shipyards, destroyers, transports that carry land units across water and unload them on a shore, and submarines that are invisible until a detector is nearby. Add a full air tier with gryphon riders and dragons that ignore terrain entirely. Implement the two-stage fog of war properly: unexplored ground is black, explored ground stays visible as terrain but hides current enemy movement, so scouting decays rather than being permanent. Let the player select up to nine units at once and give move, attack, patrol, stand-ground and harvest orders with waypoints. Upgrades bought at the blacksmith, lumber mill and stronghold must persist and apply retroactively to every existing unit of that type. Give Orcs and Humans mirrored rosters with distinct spellcasters — mage and paladin against death knight and ogre-mage, with blizzard, polymorph, healing, bloodlust and raise-dead as tactically different tools. Include two-player head-to-head multiplayer.
prompts.watchFor: No naval layer, or ships that cannot carry land units; oil missing so gold and lumber are the whole economy; submarines always visible; fog of war as a single black/visible state with no explored-but-stale shroud; upgrades applying only to newly built units; spellcasters with recoloured damage instead of distinct spells; single-unit selection; no multiplayer.

prompts.title: Heroes of Might and Magic
prompts.prompt: Build Heroes of Might and Magic as a multi-file web turn-based strategy game, and build BOTH of its layers, because the game is the tension between them. The ADVENTURE MAP is an overworld where each hero has a movement allowance per turn spent crossing terrain of differing cost, picking up resource piles, flagging mines and sawmills that then pay out every turn, visiting huts and obelisks that grant permanent bonuses, and recruiting armies. Heroes carry an army of up to five CREATURE STACKS, each stack a count of one creature type. When two heroes meet, the game cuts to the BATTLEFIELD: a separate hex grid where stacks act in initiative order, move and attack, ranged stacks suffer a penalty in melee, and the hero themself never fights but casts one spell per round from a spellbook limited by their knowledge and spell points. Each town is a build tree — you construct creature dwellings that then produce a fixed number of that creature every week, plus a mage guild that determines which spells are available, and defensive walls that appear in the battle if the town is attacked. Heroes gain levels, primary stats and artifacts. Include several distinct town factions with entirely different creature line-ups, and a weekly clock that drives growth.
prompts.watchFor: Combat resolved by comparing army totals instead of a real tactical battlefield; heroes fighting as units rather than casting; creature stacks as individual units with no stack count; dwellings producing on purchase rather than on a weekly growth tick; mines flagged but paying nothing per turn; one generic town type; movement allowance ignored so heroes cross the map in a turn; no artifacts or hero levelling.

prompts.title: Star Wars: Dark Forces
prompts.prompt: Build Star Wars: Dark Forces as a multi-file web first-person shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons, so hand-roll the camera and controls). What separated this from its contemporaries is ARCHITECTURE: build levels with genuine room-over-room verticality — catwalks above open shafts, bridges over the floor you just walked, multi-storey hangars — plus full free look up and down, jumping, crouching and ducking through low ducts. Levels must be objective-driven rather than find-the-exit mazes: the mission briefing names a goal (steal the plans, plant a charge, rescue an informant, sabotage a reactor) and the player has to navigate a large interconnected complex to achieve it, often backtracking once a switch or keycard opens a route. Give the player a headlamp with a battery for dark sections, a field-repair item, and a weapon set escalating from blaster pistol to repeater, thermal detonators and mortar. Stormtroopers should react in groups and call out, officers should trigger alarms, and some sections must reward avoiding a fight rather than winning it. Add scrolling text briefings and a mission objectives screen the player can consult mid-level.
prompts.watchFor: Flat single-storey level geometry with no room-over-room, which is the whole point; no free look up and down; levels that are corridor mazes ending at an exit switch rather than objective-driven; no mission objectives screen; headlamp and battery missing so dark areas are just unlit; enemies with identical reactions and no alarm behaviour; CDN-loaded three.js instead of the vendored copy.

prompts.title: Full Throttle
prompts.prompt: Build Full Throttle as a multi-file web point-and-click adventure with a heavy-metal biker aesthetic — dust, chrome, neon and long desert road. Replace the verb grid with the VERB COIN: hold the mouse over a hotspot and a small radial menu blooms under the cursor with eyes for look, a hand for use or pick up, a boot for kick, and a mouth for talk, and the player drags to the icon they want. That single interface change is the thing to get right; it should feel fast and physical, never like a menu. Between adventure scenes, drop into the ROAD COMBAT sections, which are not cutscenes: the player rides alongside rival gang members and must take their weapon by beating them in a short exchange, then use that weapon (chain, board, boot) against the next rider who is vulnerable to it — so the fights are a rock-paper-scissors of stolen gear rather than a reflex test. Add a demolition-derby set piece with its own rules. Keep the story cinematic through animated interstitials, give every character a distinct voice in the writing, and make dialogue trees carry the plot. Nobody can be permanently stuck, and deaths (where they exist) must rewind to just before the failure rather than to a save.
prompts.watchFor: A traditional verb grid or a text list instead of the radial verb coin; the coin implemented as a click-to-open menu that kills the flow; road fights as unskippable cutscenes or as pure reaction tests with no weapon-stealing loop; weapons that all behave identically against every rider; the derby missing; any unwinnable state; deaths that dump the player back to a save screen.

prompts.title: Quake
prompts.prompt: Build Quake as a multi-file web first-person shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). This is the jump to TRUE 3D and nothing may be faked: levels are real polygonal geometry with arbitrary angles, slopes and stacked rooms; enemies are polygonal models with animation, not billboard sprites; and the player looks freely on all axes with movement that is fully three-dimensional. Bake or precompute static lighting so rooms have real light and shadow pools rather than flat ambient. The physics must be a genuine simulation with gravity, momentum and acceleration, air control, and impulse applied by explosions — which gives you the acceptance test for this whole build: ROCKET JUMPING must work, and it must work because a rocket's splash damage applies a physical impulse to the player who fired it, never because you special-cased a move. Include the weapon set (axe, shotgun, double-barrel, nailgun, super nailgun, grenade launcher, rocket launcher, lightning gun) with distinct projectile and hitscan behaviour, monsters that pathfind in three dimensions and infight, and hazards including lava, water with drowning, and crushers. Build client-server DEATHMATCH for several players with client-side prediction and interpolation so movement stays smooth under latency.
prompts.watchFor: Billboard sprites for enemies instead of animated 3D models; level geometry restricted to axis-aligned boxes; no free vertical look; flat ambient lighting with no precomputed light and shadow; rocket jumping special-cased as a move rather than emerging from splash impulse; no player momentum or air control; multiplayer without prediction so movement rubber-bands; monsters that cannot path vertically.

prompts.title: Duke Nukem 3D
prompts.prompt: Build Duke Nukem 3D as a multi-file web first-person shooter. Model levels as Build-engine style sectors with sloped floors and ceilings and room-over-room stacking, so the world reads as real places — a cinema, a strip club, a police station, a submarine — rather than abstract corridors. The defining quality is INTERACTIVITY, and it must be pervasive enough that the player expects everything to work: light switches that actually change sector lighting, breakable glass and mirrors that reflect, working toilets and taps Duke can drink from to regain a little health, pool tables whose balls scatter, vending machines, arcade cabinets, and SECURITY CAMERAS that render a live second view onto in-world monitors — that camera-to-monitor feed is the acceptance test that the renderer is genuinely re-entrant. Give Duke the full toolkit and make each item a distinct verb: pipe bombs thrown and detonated remotely on a separate trigger, laser tripmines stuck to walls, the shrink ray that lets you stomp a shrunk enemy, the freezethrower that leaves a shatterable ice block, a jetpack with fuel, holoduke as a decoy that draws enemy fire, and steroids. Add underwater sections with air supply, destructible walls, hidden areas behind bookcases, and enemies with distinct attacks including the flying pig cops and octabrains.
prompts.watchFor: Scenery that cannot be shot, switched, broken or used, which removes the entire character of the game; no room-over-room or sloped surfaces; security monitors as static textures rather than a live rendered view; pipe bombs on a timer instead of a remote detonator; shrink and freeze as plain damage with no stomp or shatter; no underwater sections or air supply; the holoduke not actually drawing enemy fire.

prompts.title: Command & Conquer: Red Alert
prompts.prompt: Build Command & Conquer: Red Alert as a multi-file web real-time strategy game in an alternate-history 1950s. Ore is the economy: ore trucks mine ore and gem fields and haul to a refinery, but unlike a finite Tiberium field, ore slowly REGROWS from its seed tiles, so contested fields are worth holding rather than stripping. Build through a sidebar with progressive charging and a placement cursor constrained near your base, and keep the power budget global so brownouts cripple radar, defences and production. Make the Allies and Soviets asymmetric in kind, not in numbers: Allies get the Chronosphere that teleports a unit across the map, GPS satellite, mobile gap generators that hide the map from the enemy, and light fast armour; Soviets get the Iron Curtain that makes a unit briefly invulnerable, Tesla coils that need power to fire, heavy mammoth armour and paratroopers. Add a full naval layer — submarines that surface to fire, destroyers with depth charges, cruisers shelling inland, transports — because water maps must play differently. Include spies who disguise as enemy infantry and, on entering a building, steal its intel (revealing the map, resetting production, or exposing power); attack dogs that instantly kill infantry but die to anything else; and Tanya, a commando who demolishes buildings with C4. Support multiplayer skirmish for several players.
prompts.watchFor: Ore that never regrows, making it identical to Tiberium; power treated as a per-building flag rather than a global budget; the two factions differing only in unit stats; superweapons as instant damage with no charge cycle; no naval layer or submarines that never submerge; spies that just enter buildings with no intel effect; Tesla coils that fire without power; no skirmish or multiplayer mode.

prompts.title: Civilization II
prompts.prompt: Build Civilization II as a multi-file web turn-based strategy game on an ISOMETRIC world map. The combat model is the headline change from its predecessor and must be built properly: every unit has attack, defence, HIT POINTS and FIREPOWER, and a battle is resolved as a series of rounds trading hit points rather than a single coin flip, so a damaged veteran unit survives to retreat and heal, and a strong defender grinds down attackers instead of vanishing. Units gain veteran status, and terrain, fortification, river and city walls all modify defence. Add caravans that establish permanent TRADE ROUTES between distant cities, paying both ends every turn, and engineers who terraform terrain and can transform one type into another. Give cities a full improvement list with per-turn gold UPKEEP so overbuilding bankrupts you, and split the treasury with tax, luxury and science rates the player sets directly. Wonders should have effects that expire when a later technology arrives. Include the advisor council, a tech tree with real prerequisites unlocking units, buildings and governments from Despotism to Democracy with different corruption and war-weariness, and a spaceship assembled part by part for the victory. Finish with a score screen and let the player keep playing after winning.
prompts.watchFor: Single-round combat with no hit points or firepower, which is Civilization I's model; no veteran status or terrain defence modifiers; caravans absent or trade routes that pay once; buildings with no gold upkeep, removing all economic pressure; a fixed tax rate the player cannot set; wonders that never expire; a top-down square grid instead of the isometric map; spaceship victory as a single expensive purchase rather than assembled parts.

prompts.title: Fallout
prompts.prompt: Build Fallout as a multi-file web isometric role-playing game in a retro-futuristic post-nuclear wasteland. Everything hangs off SPECIAL: seven primary attributes that the player distributes at creation and that then genuinely derive the rest of the sheet — Agility sets Action Points, Intelligence sets skill points per level AND gates whole dialogue branches, Charisma sets party size, Luck triggers critical results. On top sit tagged skills that improve faster, two optional traits with a real drawback each, and a perk chosen every few levels. Combat is TURN-BASED on the same isometric map with Action Points spent on moving, attacking and reloading, plus TARGETED shots at specific body parts — eyes, arms, legs, groin — with different hit penalties and different crippling effects. The design rule that must hold everywhere: every significant quest needs at least three routes through it — fight, talk (gated on Speech and Intelligence), or sneak/steal — and a low-Intelligence character must actually speak in monosyllables and be treated differently by NPCs. Add a world map of travel between locations with random encounters, a reputation system, and an ending sequence that narrates the fate of each settlement separately based on what the player did there.
prompts.watchFor: SPECIAL attributes as cosmetic numbers that do not derive Action Points, skill points or dialogue gating; real-time combat; no targeted body-part shots or crippling; quests with a single fight-only solution; Intelligence not changing dialogue at all; a single generic ending instead of per-settlement outcomes; perks and traits with no mechanical effect; no world map travel or encounters.

prompts.title: Age of Empires
prompts.prompt: Build Age of Empires as a multi-file web real-time strategy game spanning the ancient world. Run FOUR resources — food, wood, gold and stone — and make villagers gather each from a physically distinct source with different rates and different drop-off buildings: foraging bushes, hunting animals that must be killed and then butchered before they rot, fishing from boats, farms that exhaust and must be rebuilt, chopping trees that are removed from the map, mining gold and stone veins that run out. The structural spine is AGE ADVANCEMENT: Stone, Tool, Bronze and Iron Age, each researched at the town centre for a large resource cost and each gated behind owning a required number of buildings from the previous age, unlocking whole tiers of units, buildings and upgrades on arrival. Houses cap population so expansion is mandatory. Add walls and towers that can be built anywhere, priests that convert enemy units over a channel time, siege weapons, and a naval tier. Give several civilisations meaningfully different bonuses and tech availability rather than palette swaps. The AI must gather with real villagers, advance ages on its own and attack in waves. Include a Wonder that can be built as an alternative victory condition, taking a long, loudly telegraphed time to complete.
prompts.watchFor: Fewer than four resources, or all resources gathered from one generic node; hunted animals and forage that never deplete; farms that are permanent; age advancement as a simple purchase with no building prerequisites, or ages that unlock nothing; no population cap; civilisations identical apart from colour; priests that damage rather than convert; AI income granted directly instead of gathered; no wonder victory.

prompts.title: Total Annihilation
prompts.prompt: Build Total Annihilation as a multi-file web real-time strategy game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons) for a genuine 3D heightmapped battlefield. Two things define it. First, the FLOW ECONOMY: metal and energy are not stockpiles you spend but rates you produce and consume continuously, shown as income against drain, and when you overcommit you go into deficit and every build and every weapon that costs energy simply slows down proportionally rather than failing — the player manages a throttle, not a bank balance. Reclaiming wrecks and rocks feeds metal back in, so battlefields become resources. Second, BALLISTICS ARE REAL: projectiles are physical objects that travel with velocity and gravity, artillery arcs over hills, shots can miss a moving target, and terrain elevation genuinely blocks line of fire, so a unit behind a ridge is safe from direct fire but not from a howitzer. Add radar coverage that shows blips distinct from actual vision, construction units that can assist each other's builds to stack build rate, repeatable build queues and patrol orders that automatically reclaim and repair, and hundreds of simultaneous units. Give each side a commander unit that can build anything, and whose death detonates a map-scarring nuclear explosion.
prompts.watchFor: Metal and energy as ordinary stockpiles with instant-fail purchases instead of a rate-based economy that degrades under deficit; hitscan weapons or projectiles that home, so artillery cannot miss and terrain never blocks a shot; a flat map with elevation as decoration; radar identical to vision; no reclaiming of wreckage; builders that cannot assist each other; no repeat build queues; commander death handled as a normal unit loss.

prompts.title: Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II
prompts.prompt: Build Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II as a multi-file web action game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). Blasters are the opening act; the LIGHTSABER is the point.
