Build saber melee as real swung geometry with timing — swings with wind-up and recovery, parries that deflect an incoming saber, and blaster bolts that can be batted back at the shooter — and let the player toggle between first and third person, because saber fighting needs to see the body. Force powers sit on TWO TREES: light side (heal, persuasion, protection, blinding) and dark side (grip, lightning, throw, destruction), with a pool of star points the player allocates on level up and a neutral core set available to both. Layer a MORALITY system over the whole campaign that is driven by play rather than by a menu choice: killing innocent civilians pushes the player dark, restraint and using light powers pushes them light, and the alignment determines which tree can be advanced, which of two divergent late campaigns is played, and which of the endings is reached. Build large 3D levels with real verticality, jumping and climbing puzzles, secret areas, and Force Jump and Force Speed as traversal tools that open otherwise unreachable routes. Include a saber duel against a named dark Jedi with its own reactive AI.
prompts.watchFor: The lightsaber as a reskinned melee weapon with no parry, no deflection of blaster bolts and no swing timing; no third-person toggle; Force powers as a flat unlock list rather than two competing trees with allocated points; alignment chosen from a dialogue menu instead of accumulated from play; alignment that does not change the level path, available powers or ending; Force Jump and Speed as buffs that unlock no traversal; a duel boss with a plain health bar and no reactive defence.

prompts.title: Dungeon Keeper
prompts.prompt: Build Dungeon Keeper as a multi-file web management simulation where the player is the villain. The dungeon does not get placed on open ground — it is EXCAVATED: the map begins as solid rock, the player marks tiles for digging, and imps tunnel them out over time, reinforcing walls and claiming floor tiles for their side. Rooms are then painted onto claimed floor, and room SIZE matters mechanically, since a bigger training room trains faster and a bigger lair houses more. The core loop that must be built correctly is that creatures are never purchased from a menu: they are ATTRACTED through portals by what the dungeon offers, so building a hatchery and a lair draws certain creatures, a training room and a library draw others, and if the rooms are missing nobody comes. Once there, creatures have needs and act for themselves — they eat chickens, sleep in their lair, train for experience, read in the library, brawl with each other when annoyed, and on PAYDAY they walk to the treasury and take their wages, and if the gold is not there they go on strike and eventually leave or turn on you. The player can slap a creature to hurry it at the cost of its mood, pick creatures up and drop them where needed, and POSSESS one to walk the dungeon in first person through its eyes. Add traps, doors, and hero parties that invade from entrances.
prompts.watchFor: Rooms placed on open ground with no excavation from solid rock; room size having no mechanical effect; creatures bought from a build menu instead of attracted by rooms; creatures with no needs, no autonomous behaviour and no infighting; payday absent so wages and treasury gold never matter; no possession mode; slapping with no mood cost; heroes spawning next to the player rather than invading from entrances and pathing in.

prompts.title: Half-Life
prompts.prompt: Build Half-Life as a multi-file web first-person shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). There is one rule that outranks everything else and it is the reason this game mattered: THE CAMERA IS NEVER TAKEN FROM THE PLAYER. There are no cutscenes, no letterboxing and no fade-to-black storytelling. Every narrative beat is a scripted sequence that happens in the world, in front of the player, while they remain in full control and can walk away, look elsewhere or shoot the participants. Build a scripted-sequence system that drives NPC movement, dialogue and set-piece events on triggers, and open the game with a long, unarmed, uninterrupted transit through a working facility so the world is established before a weapon is. Give the marines a squad AI that is visibly smarter than the era's monsters: they flank, use grenades to flush the player from cover, lay down suppressing fire, retreat when losing and call out to each other. Chain the levels so transitions are in-world doorways, lifts and trains rather than a menu. Include the crowbar, the physics-flavoured set pieces (a tram ride, a collapsing bridge, a tentacle that hunts by sound), an escalating alien bestiary, and headcrabs that convert corpses. Keep the HUD minimal and diegetic.
prompts.watchFor: Any cutscene that removes player control or moves the camera; story delivered by text screens between levels; scripted events that only fire if the player stands in a specific spot facing forward; marines that charge in a straight line with no flanking, grenades or retreat; level changes shown as a loading menu with a mission briefing; the opening skipped in favour of starting armed in a firefight; the sound-hunting tentacle reduced to an ordinary sight-based enemy.

prompts.title: StarCraft
prompts.prompt: Build StarCraft as a multi-file web real-time strategy game. Two resources — minerals and vespene gas, the gas requiring a refinery built on a geyser — and THREE races that must be asymmetric in their production model itself, not merely in their unit stats. Terran: SCVs build a structure by staying with it until finished and can later repair mechanical units and buildings; structures can lift off and relocate; supply comes from depots; wounded biological units need a medic. Zerg: everything hatches from LARVAE that accumulate slowly at a hatchery, so unit choice and expansion are the same decision; buildings can only be placed on creep that spreads from hatcheries and creep colonies; Overlords provide supply and are the race's only mobile detection; all units regenerate health passively. Protoss: buildings are WARPED IN remotely by a probe that leaves immediately, must sit inside a pylon's power field or shut down, every unit has a regenerating shield layer over its health, and units are individually expensive and slow to replace. Add cloaking and burrowing with detectors as the counter, high ground granting a miss chance to attackers shooting up, and unit upgrades that apply retroactively. Build a campaign across all three races and multiplayer skirmish with an AI that expands and pressures.
prompts.watchFor: Three races that share one build pipeline with different art; Zerg producing units from a building instead of from larvae; creep and pylon power fields absent or non-binding; Protoss shields as extra hit points with no separate regeneration; supply mechanisms identical across races; no detection counter to cloak and burrow; high ground with no combat effect; upgrades applying only to new units; a single shared campaign.

prompts.title: Baldur's Gate
prompts.prompt: Build Baldur's Gate as a multi-file web isometric role-playing game on hand-authored maps. Implement AD&D second-edition rules honestly rather than smoothing them into modern conveniences: THAC0 driving to-hit rolls, armour class that goes DOWN as it improves, saving throws by category, hit dice rolled on level up, class and race restrictions on what may be equipped, and VANCIAN casting where spells are memorised into a finite set of slots and are gone once cast until the party rests. Combat is REAL-TIME WITH PAUSE and the pause is the interface: the player freezes the field at will, queues an action for each of up to six party members, and unpauses to watch the round resolve, with an option to auto-pause on events like a party member wounded or a spell cast. Companions are not stat blocks — each has an alignment, opinions, banter, and will argue with or leave a party whose reputation drifts too far from their own, and reputation itself changes shop prices and whether guards attack. Build a large explorable region of hand-made wilderness and town maps connected by a travel map with timed journeys, day/night, fog of war and line of sight per party member, an inventory with weight and containers, and a quest journal that fills itself from conversations.
prompts.watchFor: Modernised rules with ascending armour class, at-will spellcasting or no rest-to-recover memorisation; turn-based or pure real-time combat with no pause-and-queue; no auto-pause conditions; companions as silent recruits with no alignment, banter or ability to leave; reputation with no effect on prices or on guards; procedurally generated maps instead of hand-authored areas; no fog of war or per-character line of sight; a journal the player must write themselves.

prompts.title: Thief: The Dark Project
prompts.prompt: Build Thief: The Dark Project as a multi-file web first-person stealth game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). LIGHT AND SOUND are simulated quantities and they are the entire game. Sample the actual light falling on the player from real light sources into a visibility meter the player can read at all times, and let them extinguish those sources — water arrows douse torches and cooking fires, and the room genuinely goes dark. Every surface carries a material with a footstep loudness: stone and tile are loud, carpet and grass are quiet, and metal is ruinous, so moss arrows fired onto a stone floor lay a silent patch. Movement speed scales noise, and creeping is slow for a reason. Guards need a graded perception model with visible states — unaware, suspicious ('did I hear something?'), actively searching with a lantern, alerted and hunting, and calling others for help — and they must return to a raised baseline afterwards rather than resetting to oblivious. Bodies must be discoverable, so a blackjacked guard has to be hidden. Make direct combat deliberately clumsy and lethal to the player, so fighting reads as failure rather than as an alternative. Add rope arrows that stick into wood for vertical routes, a loot target per mission, readable scrolls and maps that the player must orient themselves, and large open levels with several routes.
prompts.watchFor: A cone-of-vision stealth model with no actual light sampling, so shadows are decorative; torches that cannot be extinguished; footsteps at one volume regardless of surface, which makes moss arrows pointless; guards with a binary alerted/unalerted flag that resets to unaware after a timer; unconscious bodies that never get found; combat that is a viable way to clear a level; no rope arrows or vertical routes; a quest-marker map instead of an in-fiction map the player has to read.

prompts.title: Fallout 2
prompts.prompt: Build Fallout 2 as a multi-file web isometric role-playing game that keeps the SPECIAL system, tag skills, traits, perks and Action-Point turn-based combat with targeted body-part shots, then expands outward in the ways the sequel actually did. Remove the predecessor's global timer and replace urgency with a much larger, denser world: several full towns that are functioning societies with their own governments, factions, economies and internal politics — a rebuilding republic, a family-run casino city obsessed with drugs and turf, a walled elitist city that treats outsiders as contamination — where helping one faction visibly costs the player with another. Reputation must be tracked PER TOWN as well as globally, with karma titles that NPCs react to. Companions become real party members who gain levels, can be given specific weapons and armour that visibly change their sprite, and can be ordered on combat behaviour and distance. Add a drivable car with a fuel cost and a trunk that acts as mobile storage, so the world map has a logistics layer. Reactivity is the standard to hold: quests must be failable and breakable, NPCs must stay dead, and it must be possible to lock yourself out of a questline through your own choices without the game preventing it.
prompts.watchFor: A global countdown copied from the first game; towns that are quest hubs with no internal factions or politics; a single global reputation with no per-town standing; companions who never level, cannot be equipped and have no combat orders; no car or no fuel and cargo consequences; quests that cannot be failed or broken; essential NPCs made unkillable; karma titles that no NPC ever reacts to.

prompts.title: System Shock 2
prompts.prompt: Build System Shock 2 as a multi-file web immersive sim using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), set aboard a starship where almost everyone is already dead. Open with a career choice — Marine, Navy or OSA — that sets starting skills and shapes the whole run, then spend CYBER-MODULES earned from objectives on statistics, weapon proficiencies, technical skills and psionics, with everything gated behind a threshold so no single character can do it all. The mechanic that gives the game its dread is WEAPON DEGRADATION: guns wear with every shot, jam and eventually break, and keeping the pistol you like alive requires the maintenance skill, spare tools and a real decision about whether to spend them. Ammunition is scarce and typed, with anti-personnel, armour-piercing and incendiary rounds performing wildly differently against hybrids, robots and annelids, so the wrong ammo is nearly useless. Add a research system where organs harvested from corpses are analysed with chemicals to unlock damage bonuses and usable items, and psionics as a separate discipline with its own power tiers. Tell the story entirely through audio logs and email left by the dead, layer a genuine antagonist presence over it that speaks to the player and lies, and make death cost nanites at a quantum reconstruction chamber that must be activated per deck.
prompts.watchFor: Weapons that never degrade or jam, which removes the core tension; one universal ammo type, or ammo types with identical effect; skills purchasable without thresholds so one character masters everything; research absent so organs are just loot; psionics folded into the weapon skill tree; story told through cutscenes rather than found logs; free respawn with no nanite cost or per-deck activation; enemies that do not respawn or repopulate cleared decks.

prompts.title: Planescape: Torment
prompts.prompt: Build Planescape: Torment as a multi-file web isometric role-playing game where the writing IS the system. The protagonist is immortal and DEATH IS A MECHANIC, not a fail state: dying returns him to life elsewhere, sometimes costs him something, and on occasion is the only way forward — dying deliberately must be a legitimate solution to at least one problem, and the player must be able to discover that. Dialogue is the primary interface and must dwarf combat in volume and consequence. Build enormous branching conversation trees whose options are GATED ON STATS — high Wisdom unlocks insight into what someone is really saying, high Intelligence unlocks deduction and recall, high Charisma unlocks persuasion — and make those gated branches the good stuff: it must be possible to talk your way past nearly every confrontation in the game, including major ones, and to end a boss encounter entirely through conversation. Wisdom should grant experience directly, so a talker levels faster than a fighter. Memory is the plot: the protagonist recovers fragments of previous incarnations, and the recollection changes his stats and unlocks abilities. Give every companion a reason to be attached to him, resolve their arcs through dialogue, and let party members be lost through what the player says. Set it in a strange city that is deliberately not a fantasy village.
prompts.watchFor: Death as an ordinary game-over and reload; dialogue reduced to three-option menus with no stat gating; stat-gated branches that only reword the same outcome; every confrontation requiring combat, with talking as a shortcut that skips a fight rather than a full alternative resolution; no experience for conversation; the amnesia plot delivered as cutscenes rather than as recovered abilities; companions who are recruitable stat blocks with no arc; a generic fantasy setting.

prompts.title: Unreal Tournament
prompts.prompt: Build Unreal Tournament as a multi-file web arena shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). Speed is the identity: fast ground movement, dodges triggered by a double-tap in any direction, and no slowdown for aiming. Every weapon must carry a PRIMARY and an ALTERNATE fire that change its role rather than its damage — the flak cannon spraying shrapnel that ricochets up close against a lobbed explosive shell at range, the sniper rifle's instant hit against a zoom, the bio-rifle's globs that stick and pool, the rocket launcher loading multiple rockets on a held trigger. The acceptance test for whether the weapon layer is real is the SHOCK RIFLE COMBO: the alt fire launches a slow plasma ball, and hitting that ball in flight with the primary instant beam must detonate it into a large explosion, which requires the two fire modes to genuinely interact in the world. Build the game MODES as first-class systems with their own rules, scoring and maps: Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag with a returnable flag and a base, Domination with timed control points, and Assault with sequenced objectives on an attack/defend timer. The bots are the product — they need adjustable skill levels, they must play the OBJECTIVE (grab the flag, hold the point, escort), navigate with jump pads and lifts, dodge incoming fire and taunt. Wrap it in a tournament ladder with mutators.
prompts.watchFor: Alt fire as a zoom or a damage multiplier on every weapon; no shock combo, meaning the fire modes never interact; modes as deathmatch with a different scoreboard rather than distinct rules; bots that shoot but ignore flags and control points; no dodge move; movement slowed by firing; maps that ignore the vertical jump-pad and lift layer; no bot skill setting or mutators.

prompts.title: Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings
prompts.prompt: Build Age of Empires II: The Age of Kings as a multi-file web real-time strategy game across the medieval world. Keep the four resources and the four-age spine — Dark, Feudal, Castle and Imperial, each requiring both a resource cost and a count of prerequisite buildings — but build the refinements that made this the genre's high-water mark. Villagers must physically CARRY what they gather, showing it, and automatically return it to the nearest appropriate drop-off, so where the player places a mill, mining camp or lumber camp is a real optimisation decision; farms are rebuilt from food rather than being permanent. Units GARRISON inside buildings: villagers shelter in the town centre under attack, and a tower or castle with archers inside fires visibly more arrows. Add formations and stances (aggressive, defensive, stand ground, no attack) with patrol orders, walls with gates that only your own units may pass, and monks that convert enemy units over a channel with a faith cooldown and can carry relics. The civilisations are the depth: give each a genuinely different tech tree with technologies simply missing, a UNIQUE UNIT trainable only at their castle, and unique upgrades — a civilisation should feel constrained, not just bonused. Include a counter system where pikemen beat cavalry, skirmishers beat archers and mangonels punish clumps, so composition beats mass.
prompts.watchFor: Resources teleporting to a global pool instead of being carried to a drop-off building; permanent farms; no garrisoning, or towers whose arrow output does not change with occupants; civilisations that only add percentage bonuses and share one full tech tree; no unique units or castle; monks that damage instead of converting; formations and stances missing; a combat model with no counters, so the largest army always wins.

prompts.title: RollerCoaster Tycoon
prompts.prompt: Build RollerCoaster Tycoon as a multi-file web park management simulation in an isometric view. The heart of it is the TRACK BUILDER, and it must be a real one: the player lays a coaster piece by piece — straights, curves at several radii, chain lift hills, drops, banking, loops, corkscrews, brakes and block sections — and the game then SIMULATES the train on that track with actual physics, accumulating potential energy on the lift hill and spending it against gravity and friction. The acceptance test is that a badly designed coaster must STALL partway round because the player did not give it enough height, and roll back, rather than being told 'invalid layout' by a rule check. From that same simulation derive the three ratings the game lives on — Excitement, Intensity and Nausea — computed from measured forces along the ride (lateral and vertical G, airtime, speed, drops, how much scenery it passes) and used by guests to decide whether they will queue. Guests are individual named agents whose thoughts the player can read and whose happiness, hunger, thirst, nausea, tiredness and cash drive their pathing along the paths that were actually built. Add per-ride ticket pricing, shops, staff who patrol assigned areas, ride inspection intervals and breakdowns, and a scenario framework with objectives and a deadline.
prompts.watchFor: Coasters chosen from prefab templates instead of built piece by piece; ratings computed from a formula over piece counts rather than from a simulated ride; trains that always complete the circuit regardless of the layout, so height and momentum never matter; guests as a visitor counter with no individual thoughts or pathing; queues that are not physical lines; no ride breakdowns or inspection; no per-ride pricing; a sandbox with no scenario objectives or deadline.

prompts.title: Deus Ex
prompts.prompt: Build Deus Ex as a multi-file web immersive sim using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). The design law is that EVERY objective has several honest routes and the level geometry is the roleplaying system: the front door covered by a turret, a vent, a rooftop reached by crates, a sewer, a locked side door that yields to lockpicks, a keypad whose code is written in an email on someone's terminal, or a guard who can simply be talked past. Build levels so that a pure-stealth run, a pure-combat run, a hacking run and a talking run are all completable, and never gate progress behind one skill. Split character growth in two: skill points earned from exploration and objectives are spent to raise disciplines like lockpicking, electronics, rifles and swimming in discrete tiers, while NANO-AUGMENTATIONS are installed into body slots — legs, arms, torso, eyes, subdermal, cranial — where each slot offers a CHOICE OF TWO mutually exclusive augs, so building one way permanently forecloses the other. Include hackable computers with readable email that contains real passwords and plot, security cameras and turrets that can be turned against their owners, non-lethal options throughout, and conversations with branching consequences where major characters can be lost or spared. Track the player's choices and resolve them in several distinct endings.
prompts.watchFor: Levels with one viable route dressed as choice; a skill the player must have to progress at all; augmentations as a flat unlock list with no exclusive slot choice; hackable terminals that only open doors and contain no readable content; non-lethal takedowns absent or strictly worse; dialogue that branches wording but not outcome; a single ending; CDN-loaded three.js instead of the vendored copy.

prompts.title: Diablo II
prompts.prompt: Build Diablo II as a multi-file web isometric action RPG. The loot engine is the game and it must be a real generator, not a hand-written drop table: items roll a quality tier (normal, magic, rare, set, unique), and magic and rare items then roll AFFIXES from prefix and suffix pools whose availability and magnitude are gated by the item's level and the level of the monster that dropped it, so the same base sword can come out as junk or as a build-defining weapon. Items have sockets that take gems and runes, and specific ordered rune combinations in the right base form RUNEWORDS with effects far beyond their parts. Give each class a three-branch SKILL TREE where points are spent permanently, higher tiers are gated behind prerequisites and level, and skills have SYNERGIES so investing in one passively strengthens another — which is what makes builds rather than shopping lists. Structure the world as fixed acts with procedurally generated maps inside them, so layouts differ every run while landmarks do not. Add three difficulty tiers that replay the same acts with higher monster levels and stacking resistance penalties, monster affixes that create dangerous elite packs, gold, gambling, a stash, and hardcore mode where death is permanent.
prompts.watchFor: A fixed drop table with hand-written items instead of a rolling affix generator; affixes not gated by item and monster level; sockets, gems and runewords missing; skill trees as a flat unlock list with no prerequisites or synergies; fully hand-authored maps with no procedural generation, or fully random maps with no fixed landmarks; one difficulty; elite monster packs with more health instead of affixes; no hardcore mode.

prompts.title: The Sims
prompts.prompt: Build The Sims as a multi-file web life simulation in an isometric house. Each Sim carries eight MOTIVES — hunger, comfort, hygiene, bladder, energy, fun, social and room — that decay continuously in real time and whose lowest values dominate mood. The architecture that must be built, because it is what makes the game feel alive rather than scripted, is ADVERTISING OBJECTS: every object in the world broadcasts what it can do for each motive and how strongly, and an autonomous Sim chooses its next action by scanning those advertisements, weighting them by its current needs and by distance, and picking the best — so behaviour EMERGES from the furniture the player bought rather than from a hardcoded routine. Add a build and buy mode with walls, doors, windows, floors, wallpaper and furniture that has price, quality and a room-score contribution, so a well-decorated room raises mood. Sims hold jobs on a career ladder with a daily carpool they must catch, required skills they build by practising at objects, and friendships they must maintain or lose. Track relationships as a value per pair driven by interaction outcomes, and let the player queue actions while the Sim still acts on its own when idle. Failure should be mundane and funny: exhaustion, fires, the social worker.
prompts.watchFor: Motives that decay but do not drive behaviour; autonomous action chosen by a hardcoded priority list or state machine rather than by objects advertising scores; objects with no motive advertisements, making buy mode cosmetic; no room score, so decoration is pointless; careers as a passive income number with no carpool or skill requirement; relationships that never decay; a Sim that only ever does what the player clicks.

prompts.title: Counter-Strike
prompts.prompt: Build Counter-Strike as a multi-file web tactical multiplayer shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). The round structure is everything and must not be softened: teams start each round at their spawn, and a dead player STAYS DEAD until the round ends, spectating. That single rule is what makes every engagement matter. Rounds end on elimination, on the bomb detonating, on a defuse, or on the timer. Run a carried-over ECONOMY: kills and round outcomes pay money, losing streaks pay escalating consolation, and each round opens with a buy window at spawn where players spend on weapons, armour, grenades and a defuse kit — so a team that loses its guns is economically punished for rounds afterwards and must decide whether to save. Model shooting with real weapon behaviour rather than a crosshair and a hit chance: each automatic weapon needs a deterministic SPRAY PATTERN that walks the shots in a learnable path, first-shot accuracy that degrades while moving or in the air, and a hard accuracy penalty until the player comes to a stop. Add the bomb plant and defuse with audible timers, one-way and mid-map audio cues from footsteps that differ when walking, hostage or bomb maps, friendly fire, and asymmetric terrorist and counter-terrorist arsenals.
prompts.watchFor: Respawning during a round; no buy phase or an economy that resets each round; accuracy identical whether standing, moving or jumping; random cone spread instead of a learnable deterministic spray pattern; the bomb as an instant objective with no plant and defuse timers; footsteps with no volume difference between walking and running; both teams sharing one weapon list; no friendly fire.

prompts.title: Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn
prompts.prompt: Build Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn as a multi-file web isometric role-playing game that keeps AD&D second-edition rules and real-time-with-pause party combat, then does what the sequel actually did: start the party at high level and make the high-level rules the content. The acceptance test is the MAGE DUEL. Implement the spell-protection stack faithfully — Stoneskin, Mirror Image, Spell Deflection, Spell Turning, Minor Globe of Invulnerability, Spell Immunity, Protection from Magical Weapons — and the counter-magic that strips it — Breach, Pierce Magic, Secret Word, Ruby Ray of Reversal, Spell Thrust — so that beating an enemy mage is a legible puzzle of identifying which layers are up and removing them in the correct order, and simply attacking accomplishes nothing. Add specialist mage kits and class kits with real trade-offs, and High Level Abilities at the top of the curve. Give companions full arcs: banter that fires on timers and locations, quarrels that can end in one killing another, romances that advance through conversation over time and can be failed, and personal quests. Give each class a STRONGHOLD with its own questline and responsibilities. Build the city as a dense hub of optional content with a strong, personal antagonist who acts on his own schedule.
prompts.watchFor: Enemy mages as damage sponges with no protection stack, which erases the game's signature encounter; counter-magic spells missing or working as generic dispel; companion banter absent or fired only in conversation with the player; romances as a single dialogue flag; no strongholds; kits that are cosmetic titles; high-level play that is just bigger numbers with no new abilities; the antagonist appearing only in the opening and finale.

prompts.title: Max Payne
prompts.prompt: Build Max Payne as a multi-file web third-person noir shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). BULLET TIME is the mechanic and there is a precise way to get it right: activating it slows the world's timescale — enemy movement, bullets in flight, animations — while the player's AIM RATE stays at full speed, so the slowdown is a genuine advantage rather than everything simply moving slower together. It runs off a finite meter that drains while active and refills only by killing enemies, so it must be spent aggressively. Pair it with the SHOOTDODGE: a committed dive in a chosen direction that enters slow motion for its duration, during which Max cannot steer or stop, can fire freely, and lands prone and vulnerable — commitment is the cost. Show bullets as visible tracers and let the camera swing behind a shot for kill flourishes. Tell the story in GRAPHIC-NOVEL PANELS — static illustrated pages with lettered captions and speech that the player advances at their own pace — instead of cutscenes. Health is restored only by painkillers found and carried, with no regeneration. Add surreal nightmare levels built as narrow trails over darkness with disorienting audio, destructible clutter, and a hard-boiled first-person narration running under everything.
prompts.watchFor: Bullet time that slows the player's aiming as much as the world, making it useless; a bullet-time meter that recharges on a timer instead of by kills; shootdodge steerable mid-dive or cancellable, removing the commitment; regenerating health instead of painkillers; story told as animated cutscenes rather than graphic-novel panels; no visible bullet tracers; nightmare levels dropped.

prompts.title: Civilization III
prompts.prompt: Build Civilization III as a multi-file web turn-based strategy game that adds the two systems this entry is remembered for. First, CULTURE: every city accumulates culture from its buildings and wonders, and that culture pushes out a visible territorial BORDER, so land is claimed by civic development rather than only by settling; borders collide and the stronger culture pushes the weaker back; and a city with overwhelming foreign culture nearby can CULTURE FLIP and defect to the other civilisation outright, losing you the city without a shot. Second, STRATEGIC RESOURCES: iron, horses, saltpetre, coal, oil, rubber, uranium and aluminium appear as finite map deposits that must be inside your borders and connected to your capital by road or harbour, and the corresponding units simply cannot be built without them — no iron means no swordsmen at any price — while luxury resources supply happiness. This makes the diplomacy screen a real trading floor where technologies, resources, gold per turn, maps and treaties are haggled as a package with AI counter-offers. Add corruption and waste scaling with distance from the palace, workers who build roads, irrigation and mines, armies that stack veteran units under a leader, and several victory conditions including cultural, diplomatic, conquest and space race.
prompts.watchFor: Cities with a fixed work radius and no expanding cultural border; no culture flipping; strategic resources present as bonus yields rather than as hard build prerequisites; resources that do not need a road connection to the capital; diplomacy as accept-or-decline with no counter-offers or multi-item trades; no corruption by distance; a single victory condition; workers absent so terrain never improves.

prompts.title: Return to Castle Wolfenstein
prompts.prompt: Build Return to Castle Wolfenstein as a multi-file web first-person shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), with a single-player campaign of occult wartime horror and — more importantly — the class-based multiplayer that outlived it. In multiplayer, teams attack and defend a SEQUENCED OBJECTIVE CHAIN on each map: blow the wall, then steal the documents, then escort them to the transmitter, with the defenders trying to hold each stage and the attackers gaining a forward spawn as stages fall. Respawns come in TIMED WAVES rather than instantly, so dying costs the team tempo and pushes coordinated assaults. Four classes with genuinely different jobs: the Soldier carries the heavy weapons, the MEDIC revives downed teammates and hands out health packs, the ENGINEER is the only class that can plant and defuse the dynamite the objectives depend on and who repairs and builds, and the Lieutenant resupplies ammo and calls in air strikes and artillery. Make the classes interdependent so a team without an engineer cannot win. Add limb-based damage, leaning around corners, weapon heat on the machine gun, and a stamina bar for sprinting. In single player, include stealth missions that fail on being detected, and an escalating supernatural bestiary.
prompts.watchFor: Instant individual respawn instead of timed waves; a single capture-the-flag objective rather than a sequenced chain with moving spawns; classes that differ only in starting weapon; medics who heal but cannot revive; engineers not required for the objective; no ammo or health resupply loop, so support classes are pointless; no leaning; stealth missions that can be brute-forced by shooting everyone.

prompts.title: Gothic
prompts.prompt: Build Gothic as a multi-file web open-world role-playing game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), set inside a single seamless penal colony sealed under a magical barrier. The defining rule, and the one that must not be softened: THERE IS NO LEVEL SCALING. The world is statically dangerous, a single wolf will kill a new character, and the player's progress comes from learning where they can and cannot go — so early exploration is about retreat, routes and cowardice, and the same path becomes trivial forty levels later. Second: the player must JOIN one of three rival camps, and that choice is a real fork — it gates the questline, the teachers available, the equipment, and how the rest of the colony treats them. Third: skills are not bought from a menu. Experience gives learning points, but a point only becomes an ability by finding a specific TRAINER NPC who teaches that thing, travelling to them and paying, so character growth is a journey through the world's social map. Build stamina-and-timing melee where attacks chain into combos on correct timing and blocking matters, and give NPCs full daily schedules — they work, eat, drink, sleep, and will confront, beat and rob the player for trespassing or stealing rather than turning hostile forever.
prompts.watchFor: Enemies that scale to the player's level, which destroys the entire progression; camps as a cosmetic faction badge that does not gate quests, trainers or gear; skills purchasable from a menu with no trainer to find; click-spam combat with no stamina, timing or blocking; NPCs standing in place with no schedules; the world split into loading zones rather than one seamless colony; being killed by any crime instead of being beaten and robbed.

prompts.title: Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis
prompts.prompt: Build Operation Flashpoint: Cold War Crisis as a multi-file web military simulation using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). Two commitments define it. First, SCALE AND LETHALITY: build large open terrain measured in square kilometres with real view distance, ballistics with travel time and bullet drop that must be led and elevated at range, and a damage model where one or two rounds incapacitate — no health regeneration, no hit markers, no crosshair for aimed fire, just iron sights, wounds that degrade your aim and movement, and the fact that you will often be killed by someone you never saw. Second, EVERYTHING IS THE SAME SIMULATION: every jeep, truck, tank, helicopter and plane on the map is genuinely drivable and flyable by the player with the same physics the AI uses, and any vehicle can be entered by seat. Put the player in a SQUAD as an ordinary rifleman who receives orders from an AI leader over a radio menu, and later have them give those same orders to their own squad with a full command interface for movement, formation, engagement rules and targets. The battle must be bigger than the player: armour columns, artillery and aircraft operating on their own elsewhere on the map, objectives that can be won or lost without them, and missions that continue after failure rather than resetting.
prompts.watchFor: A corridor level dressed as open terrain; hitscan weapons with no travel time or drop; regenerating health or a hit-marker crosshair; vehicles as fixed rail sequences or scenery; the player unable to take any seat in a vehicle; no squad command interface; a battlefield where nothing happens outside the player's mission trigger; instant mission restart on death instead of a campaign that carries the outcome.

prompts.title: The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind
prompts.prompt: Build The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind as a multi-file web open-world role-playing game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), in a setting that is deliberately alien — giant fungal towers, insect transport, ash wastes — rather than generic fantasy. Navigation is the identity: there are NO QUEST MARKERS and no click-to-travel. Directions are given in conversation in plain language and written verbatim into the player's JOURNAL, so finding a place means reading 'follow the road north from Balmora past the standing stone, then east at the ridge' and actually doing it, with travel by foot, silt strider, boat, guild teleport and mark-and-recall spells. Skills advance BY USE — swinging a blade raises Blade, casting raises the relevant school — and levelling multiplies attributes based on which skills were used, so growth follows behaviour. The other pillar is player-authored magic: build spellmaking and enchanting as combinatorial systems where the player selects EFFECTS, magnitudes, durations and areas from what they have learned and pays a computed cost, creating spells and enchanted items the designers never wrote. Let that be exploitable — a self-made levitation or intervention spell breaking a quest open is a feature. Add faction questlines with rank requirements, readable in-world books, and dice-rolled melee where skill governs whether a swing connects.
prompts.watchFor: Quest markers, a compass arrow or fast travel by clicking the map, all of which delete the game's core experience; directions summarised as an objective line instead of written into a journal; skills that level from experience points rather than from use; spellmaking and enchanting absent or reduced to buying fixed spells; systems patched to prevent exploits; a conventional fantasy setting; books as flavour props that cannot be read.

prompts.title: Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos
prompts.prompt: Build Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos as a multi-file web real-time strategy game whose whole balance points away from mass armies and toward a small elite force led by a HERO. Heroes are persistent units that gain experience and LEVELS, carry a six-slot INVENTORY of items they pick up off the ground, and have three spells plus an ultimate unlocked by level, with a skill point spent per level — so a hero is a growing character, not a strong unit. To force that focus, implement UPKEEP: once a player's food usage crosses defined thresholds, their gold INCOME IS TAXED at increasing rates, so a bigger army literally makes you poorer, and the acceptance test is that a player at high upkeep visibly earns less per trip than one below it. Populate the map with neutral CREEP camps guarding gold mines, item drops and shops, which must be cleared for hero experience — making the early game about farming neutral monsters, not rushing the enemy. Add a day/night cycle where night reduces vision and lets creeps sleep, allowing safe passage. Give four asymmetric races with different worker and expansion models, and a campaign that carries heroes and their items between missions.
prompts.watchFor: Heroes as a stronger unit with no levels, skill points or item inventory; no upkeep, or upkeep that does not reduce income, which returns the game to mass-unit play; a map with no neutral creep camps or creeps that give no experience; no item drops or shops; day and night as a lighting filter with no vision or creep-sleep effect; four races sharing one economy model; a campaign that resets the hero every mission.

prompts.title: Battlefield 1942
prompts.prompt: Build Battlefield 1942 as a multi-file web multiplayer shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), on maps large enough that crossing them on foot is a poor idea. CONQUEST is the mode: the map is dotted with capturable CONTROL POINTS that a team takes by standing near them, and each captured point becomes a SPAWN POINT, so territory is literally where you come back to life and the front line moves as points change hands. Each team holds a TICKET count that bleeds continuously while the enemy holds more points and drops on each death, so losing map control loses the match without a single elimination. Vehicles are first-class and SHARED: tanks, jeeps, half-tracks, fighters, bombers, destroyers, battleships, submarines and aircraft carriers are all spawnable at bases, and multi-crew vehicles have distinct seats other players occupy — a pilot with a rear gunner, a tank driver with a separate turret gunner, a jeep with a mounted machine gun — with the seats visible and enterable. Give four or five kits with distinct roles including an engineer who repairs vehicles and an anti-tank class, add parachutes, and let planes take off from and land on carriers. Vehicles must be destructible and respawn on a timer at their base.
prompts.watchFor: Vehicles as single-seat pickups with no shared crew positions; control points that grant score but are not spawn points; no ticket bleed, so the match ends only on kills; maps small enough to make vehicles pointless; kits that differ only in weapon; engineers who cannot repair; aircraft on rails or with no landing; vehicles that never run out or respawn instantly next to the player.

prompts.title: Mafia
prompts.prompt: Build Mafia as a multi-file web narrative crime game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), set in a fully drivable 1930s American city. This is not a sandbox of chaos: the story is a LINEAR sequence of authored missions telling one man's rise and fall, and the open city exists to make them feel real. The defining decision, and the one that must be kept, is that the CITY HAS LAWS AND THEY APPLY TO THE PLAYER: there is a speed limit, and police will pull the player over and ticket them for speeding, running a red light, damaging property or driving a visibly damaged car — so the drive to a job is a tense, deliberate, law-abiding journey rather than a demolition derby, and the player learns to obey traffic signals. Model the cars accordingly: heavy, slow, period-accurate top speeds, feeble brakes, real weight transfer, fuel that runs out, and damage that degrades handling. Add a mission where the player must win a period race under full simulation rules. Build shooting as slow and deadly with iron sights and no regeneration, keep cutscenes cinematic and character-driven, and offer a separate Free Ride mode for players who just want the city.
prompts.watchFor: A city with no traffic law enforcement, which turns it into a generic sandbox; arcade car handling with modern grip, brakes and speed; no fuel or damage model; the story restructured as free-roaming optional missions; regenerating health and forgiving gunfights; police that only react to shooting; no Free Ride mode; a city that is a backdrop rather than fully drivable.

prompts.title: Neverwinter Nights
prompts.prompt: Build Neverwinter Nights as a multi-file web role-playing game on third-edition D&D rules — feats, skill ranks, multiclassing, attacks of opportunity, iterative attacks at high base attack bonus, and a visible d20 combat log showing every roll against its target number — with a campaign playable solo alongside a hired henchman. But the deliverable that actually defines this game is the TOOLSET, and it must ship as part of the build: an in-browser module editor where the player creates areas by painting from tilesets, places creatures, items, doors, placeables and triggers, writes branching CONVERSATION TREES with condition and action hooks, sets encounters and waypoints, and wires simple scripted events — then saves the whole thing as a module file that can be loaded and PLAYED in the same application, and exported to share. The acceptance test is exactly that round trip: build a small module in the editor, save it, load it, and play it through to its ending. Add multiplayer where several players join one module together, with one participant acting as a DUNGEON MASTER who can possess creatures, spawn encounters, adjust the world live and speak as any NPC.
prompts.watchFor: No toolset, which reduces this to a generic D&D game; a toolset that cannot save or reload a module, or whose output is not playable in the app; conversation editing limited to plain text with no branching, conditions or actions; simplified rules with no feats, multiclassing or attacks of opportunity; no combat log showing rolls; no multiplayer, or multiplayer with no dungeon-master role; henchman that cannot be equipped or commanded.

prompts.title: Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic
prompts.prompt: Build Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic as a multi-file web role-playing game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). Underneath the action-looking presentation must sit a genuine d20 TURN ENGINE: combat runs in rounds with attack rolls, defence, damage dice, saving throws and feats, resolved on a real timer and pausable so the player queues each party member's actions, with a combat log the player can open to see every roll. Nothing may be resolved by twitch aiming. Layer LIGHT AND DARK SIDE alignment over everything, moved by dialogue and deeds rather than by a menu setting, and make it mechanical: Force powers cost more to use against your alignment, some powers are gated entirely, and your appearance changes as you fall. Build a party of companions with distinct voices and their own quests that unlock as their opinion of the player rises — and let that opinion be driven by whether the player's choices match their outlook, so an alignment run changes who opens up. Give the player a ship and a galaxy map with several planets tackled in any order, each a self-contained story with a moral fork that has no clean answer. Structure the whole plot so a late revelation recontextualises the protagonist's identity, and let the player's alignment at that moment change what happens next.
prompts.watchFor: Real-time action combat with aimed shots instead of a paused d20 round engine; no combat log; alignment as a slider set in a menu with no effect on power cost or availability; companions who never comment and whose quests unlock on a timer instead of on approval; planets locked into a fixed order; a moral choice system that is only ever obviously good or obviously evil; the late revelation as a cutscene with no branching consequence.

prompts.title: Call of Duty
prompts.prompt: Build Call of Duty as a multi-file web wartime first-person shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). The premise that separates it from its contemporaries is that THE PLAYER IS NEVER ALONE and never the whole army: AI squadmates advance beside them, shout callouts, take cover, get killed, and the level moves at the squad's pace. Build the signature pressure system honestly — enemies reinforce continuously from spawn points behind a line, and that flow only stops when the player and their squad ADVANCE past a trigger, so sitting in cover and killing everything is impossible by design and the game teaches forward movement under fire. Present the war from three national campaigns — American, British and Soviet — that cover the same conflict from different sides, and include a Soviet mission where the player is sent forward without a rifle and must take one from a fallen soldier. Sell the chaos with suppression: incoming near-misses blur and deafen the player's senses temporarily, artillery shakes the screen and leaves ringing, and grenades are indicated so they can be avoided. Health is a limited pool restored by med-kits, not by waiting. Add scripted set pieces that never take the camera away, iron-sight aiming on the weapons that had it, and multiplayer deathmatch and objective modes.
prompts.watchFor: A lone-wolf level with no squadmates or with squadmates who cannot be killed; finite enemy counts that reward camping in cover instead of a spawn flow tied to player advance; one campaign instead of three national perspectives; no suppression, deafening or screen-shake feedback; regenerating health; cutscenes that take camera control; scripted events that fire regardless of where the squad actually is.

prompts.title: SimCity 4
prompts.prompt: Build SimCity 4 as a multi-file web city-building simulation, isometric over terrain with real elevation. Two systems make this the deepest of its line. First, the REGION: the playable area is a large map cut into separate city tiles that are developed one at a time, and neighbouring cities are real neighbours — they trade power, water and garbage disposal under negotiated deals, their road, rail and highway connections must line up at the shared border, and commuters cross between them, so a player can deliberately build a residential suburb next to an industrial city. Second, and more important, the simulation is AGENT-BASED: individual sims live in a specific house and work at a specific job, and every day they PATHFIND along the actual road and transit network to get there. Traffic congestion is the emergent result of those trips, and if a route is too slow or missing, the sim cannot reach work, the job goes unfilled and the industrial building abandons — so road layout is not decoration, it is the economy. Model demand for residential, commercial and industrial at three WEALTH LEVELS with separate desirability driven by land value, pollution, crime, education and health coverage, all viewable as data overlay maps. Add a budget with per-department funding and per-zone tax rates, ordinances, zoning density, and a query tool on every building.
prompts.watchFor: A single isolated city with no region or neighbour connections; commuting modelled as a statistical percentage rather than agents pathfinding the built network, so traffic never emerges and road layout does not matter; one undifferentiated wealth level for zones; no data overlay maps; terrain without elevation; funding sliders with no visible service coverage effect; buildings that never abandon.

prompts.title: EVE Online
prompts.prompt: Build a playable web slice of EVE Online as a multi-file game — a handful of connected star systems rather than a galaxy — that preserves the systems the real game is actually famous for, since a full clone is not the point. First and above all, a PLAYER-DRIVEN MARKET: every station hosts a regional ORDER BOOK where participants post buy and sell orders with a price, a quantity, a duration and a range, and trades execute by matching those orders, so every price in the game is set by participants and there is no vendor price list anywhere. Show order history and price graphs, and let the player profit purely by hauling goods between systems at different prices. Second, CONSEQUENCE: destruction is permanent and total — a lost ship and everything fitted to it is gone, dropping a partial wreck the killer can loot — so undocking is always a risk calculation. Third, SHIP FITTING as a constraint puzzle: hulls provide high, mid and low slots plus finite CPU and powergrid, and every module consumes both, so a fit is an optimisation rather than a shopping list. Fourth, SKILL TRAINING IN REAL TIME: skills train on a wall clock queue whether or not the player is active, gating what can be flown and fitted. Close the loop with mining, refining into minerals, and manufacturing from blueprints that consume those minerals.
prompts.watchFor: An NPC vendor with fixed prices instead of a player order book; a market that is a single global list with no regional separation or hauling opportunity; destroyed ships refunded, respawned or insured to full value; fitting with unlimited slots or no CPU and powergrid constraint; skills trained by grinding activity rather than on a real-time queue; manufacturing that creates items from gold with no mined material inputs; the slice expanded into a shallow galaxy instead of a deep few systems.

prompts.title: Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne
prompts.prompt: Build Max Payne 2: The Fall of Max Payne as a multi-file web third-person noir shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). Keep bullet time decoupling world timescale from the player's aim rate, and keep the committed shootdodge, then build the sequel's refinement: bullet time now REWARDS AGGRESSION. Killing an enemy while slow motion is active refills the meter, and as the meter fills Max's own reload, turn and weapon-swap animations speed UP relative to the slowed world, so a player chaining kills accelerates into a state where he is visibly faster than everything around him. That escalating feedback loop is the acceptance test — a good player should be able to sustain slow motion indefinitely while a poor one runs dry immediately. The second pillar is a full RIGID-BODY PHYSICS layer applied to the whole world: bodies ragdoll and slide realistically, and levels are deliberately littered with dynamic clutter — boxes, bottles, chairs, paint cans, hanging signs — that reacts to gunfire, to explosions and to Max diving through it, so every firefight physically wrecks the room. Keep the graphic-novel panel storytelling and hard-boiled narration, add levels where an AI companion fights alongside and can be lost, and make painkillers the only healing.
prompts.watchFor: Bullet time recharging on a timer rather than by kills scored inside it; no animation speed-up as the meter fills, which removes the escalation; canned death animations instead of ragdoll physics; static scenery that ignores bullets and explosions; levels with no dynamic clutter to wreck; regenerating health; story told as animated cutscenes rather than illustrated panels; the AI companion invulnerable or scripted.

prompts.title: Half-Life 2
prompts.prompt: Build Half-Life 2 as a multi-file web first-person shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons) with a real rigid-body physics engine at its centre. Physics here is not decoration, it is a PUZZLE LANGUAGE: build encounters solved by mass, buoyancy, leverage and constraint — a ramp that must be counterweighted with cinder blocks before a vehicle can climb it, a see-saw bridge, a cage lifted by loading barrels underneath it, a plank floated across water. The GRAVITY GUN is the verb that makes the language usable: it pulls any dynamic object to the player at range and fires it away with force, so sawblades, radiators and barrels become both tools and weapons, and its final upgraded form should change how the endgame is fought. Keep the series' absolute rule that the camera is NEVER taken from the player — no cutscenes, no fades, no loss of control — with all story delivered by characters who talk to the player in the world while they are free to walk off. Add long vehicle sections with real suspension physics over open coastal terrain, an AI companion who fights competently and must be kept alive in places, soldiers with squad tactics who flank and use grenades, and expressive facial animation on the characters delivering dialogue.
prompts.watchFor: Physics objects that are cosmetic debris with no puzzle role; puzzles solved by a hidden switch dressed as physics; a gravity gun restricted to marked objects instead of anything dynamic; any cutscene or loss of camera control; vehicle sections on rails; a companion who is invulnerable or who contributes nothing; soldiers who charge in a line with no flanking or grenades; dialogue delivered to a locked camera.

prompts.title: World of Warcraft
prompts.prompt: Build a playable web slice of World of Warcraft as a multi-file game — a couple of connected zones, a capital and one dungeon, rather than a continent — preserving the systems that made it the template. Levelling is QUEST-DRIVEN: a quest log holds objectives that track automatically, quest givers are marked in the world, and zones are laid out as a chain of quest hubs that pull the player along a level curve, so questing is the fastest progression rather than grinding mobs. Build the HOLY TRINITY on top of an explicit THREAT system — the acceptance test for the whole combat model — where every point of damage, healing and certain abilities generate threat recorded in a per-enemy table, the enemy always attacks whoever is highest on its table, tanks have abilities that multiply their threat generation, and damage dealers who overtake the tank get killed. Nothing about tanking may be a scripted taunt flag. Add classes with several TALENT TREES that specialise them into different roles, a global cooldown, gear with stat budgets and rarity tiers, an instanced five-player DUNGEON with mechanics requiring crowd control and positioning, a player-run auction house, professions, and seamless zones with no loading between them.
prompts.watchFor: Aggro handled as nearest-target or a scripted taunt rather than an accumulating per-enemy threat table; healers and tanks that have no way to hold or shed threat; quests that are kill counters with no log, tracking or hub structure; a single talent path per class; the dungeon as a corridor of tougher mobs with no mechanics; vendor-priced items instead of a player auction house; zones separated by loading screens.

prompts.title: Rome: Total War
prompts.prompt: Build Rome: Total War as a multi-file web strategy game that is genuinely TWO GAMES joined at the seam, and both must be built. The campaign layer is turn-based on a map of provinces: armies and agents move with a movement allowance, cities are developed through building queues that unlock troop types, a family tree ages, produces heirs and generals who acquire traits and retinues from their deeds, the senate hands out missions that can be obeyed or defied, and diplomats, spies and assassins operate between factions. When two armies meet the game drops into a REAL-TIME 3D BATTLE of thousands of soldiers on the terrain of that province, and here the acceptance test is that MORALE, NOT HIT POINTS, decides battles. Every unit tracks morale affected by fatigue, casualties, being flanked or charged in the rear, losing its general, facing elephants or fire, and holding high ground — and when morale breaks the unit ROUTS and physically flees the field, and a rout must be contagious, cascading through nearby friendly units so an army collapses rather than being killed to the last man. Model formations, unit facing, charge bonuses that depend on impact speed, fatigue that accumulates from running and fighting in heat, and missile troops that need line of sight and can hit their own men.
prompts.watchFor: Only one of the two layers built; battles auto-resolved by comparing army strength; morale absent so units fight to the last man; routing units that vanish instead of fleeing, or routs that never spread; unit facing and flanking with no combat effect; charges that do the same damage from a standstill; fatigue and terrain elevation ignored; generals with no traits or family tree; a senate that issues no missions.

prompts.title: Unreal Tournament 2004
prompts.prompt: Build Unreal Tournament 2004 as a multi-file web arena shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), keeping the dual-fire weapon set and the shock rifle combo, and adding the movement and the mode that define this entry. Movement gains a double jump and the DODGE-JUMP — a dodge chained immediately into a jump for a long, fast, low leap — so expert traversal is a distinct skill from shooting, and adrenaline collected around the map can be spent by typing a short directional combo to trigger booster, speed, invisibility or berserk. The headline mode is ONSLAUGHT and it must be built as a real graph: the map holds a network of POWER NODES linked in a fixed topology between two power cores, and a team can only attack a node that is currently LINKED to something it already owns, so the match is a moving front along a graph rather than a free-for-all of capture points. Nodes are built and destroyed by weapon fire, and taking one advances the team's spawn. Vehicles carry the mode — a fast hoverbike, an attack aircraft, a heavy tank, a multi-seat troop vehicle and a huge siege walker — with driver and passenger seats and vehicles that must be driven across large terrain maps. The bots must play Onslaught properly: choosing linked nodes, driving vehicles and defending.
prompts.watchFor: Onslaught as generic capture points with no link topology or attack restriction; nodes captured by standing near them instead of being built and destroyed; vehicles absent or single-seat only; no double jump or dodge-jump; adrenaline collected but with no combo input; bots that ignore nodes and vehicles; maps too small for the vehicle layer to matter; alt-fire reduced to a zoom.

prompts.title: Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines
prompts.prompt: Build Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines as a multi-file web role-playing game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), across a few dense night-time city hubs. CLAN CHOICE at character creation must reshape the actual game rather than adjust statistics, and this is the acceptance test: choose Nosferatu and the character is so monstrous that being SEEN by any human is an immediate violation, so entire routes through the city must exist through sewers and rooftops that other clans never need; choose Malkavian and the dialogue text itself is REWRITTEN into deranged, prophetic non-sequiturs across the whole game, with unique lines and unique reactions; Toreador get social options, Brujah get brute force, Ventrue cannot feed on the poor and must hunt selectively, Tremere get blood sorcery. Enforce the MASQUERADE as a running meter: feeding, using visible powers or drawing weapons in front of humans costs violations, each one drawing consequences, and exhausting it ends the game outright. Blood is both health and the fuel for disciplines, so surviving means hunting, and feeding too deeply kills the victim, which is itself a violation. Build quests with several resolutions gated on Persuasion, Seduction, Intimidation and Dominate, a haven the player returns to, and endings determined by which faction they backed.
prompts.watchFor: Clans as stat packages with identical dialogue and identical level routing; Nosferatu with no alternate sewer and rooftop routes; Malkavian dialogue unchanged or limited to a few jokes; a Masquerade meter that never actually fails the game; blood as a plain mana bar disconnected from health and feeding; feeding with no risk of killing the victim; quests with a single combat resolution; one ending regardless of faction.

prompts.title: Civilization IV
prompts.prompt: Build Civilization IV as a multi-file web turn-based strategy game — the entry that refined the formula through three new systems, all of which must be present. RELIGION: each of several religions is founded by whichever civilisation first researches its associated technology, then SPREADS city to city passively and through missionary units, granting culture and gold at its holy city, enabling temples and monasteries, and creating diplomatic blocs where sharing a state religion warms relations and differing ones sour them. CIVICS: government is replaced by five independent categories — legal, labour, economy, religion and government — each offering several options the player mixes freely, with per-turn upkeep costs and anarchy when switching, so a nation's politics is a build rather than a single label. GREAT PEOPLE: cities employing specialists accumulate great person points and periodically produce a named Great Prophet, Artist, Scientist, Engineer or Merchant who may be spent once — bulbing a technology instantly, building a wonder outright, starting a golden age, or settling permanently in a city for ongoing yield. Add health and unhealthiness tracked separately from happiness, unit PROMOTIONS chosen on combat experience, a tech tree with multiple prerequisites per technology, and corporations of trade.
prompts.watchFor: Religion as a flavour label that never spreads or affects diplomacy; a single government dropdown instead of mixed civics with upkeep and anarchy; great people generated randomly rather than from specialists, or with a single generic effect; health folded into happiness; units that never earn promotions; a linear tech tree with one prerequisite per technology; no holy cities or missionaries.

prompts.title: F.E.A.R.
prompts.prompt: Build F.E.A.R. as a multi-file web first-person shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). The ENEMY AI is the product, and it must be a real planner rather than a set of triggers: give each soldier goals (kill the player, stay alive, maintain squad cohesion) and a library of actions with preconditions and effects, and let them SEARCH for a valid action sequence at runtime — so when a soldier needs to attack and has no line of fire, it works out that it must first relocate, and the specific route it takes is derived, not scripted. The behaviour that must emerge from this: squads flanking through side rooms while others suppress, soldiers vaulting over railings, kicking over tables and filing cabinets to create cover where none exists, blind-firing from behind cover, retreating when losing and regrouping, and calling their intentions aloud so the player can hear a flank being organised. The acceptance test is that a soldier announces a manoeuvre and then genuinely performs it against the current geometry, in a level the AI has never seen scripted. Pair this with REFLEX TIME — a finite slow-motion meter that leaves the player's aim at full speed — and make firefights physically wreck the room with dense particles, ricochets, sparks, plaster and shattering glass. Interleave silent supernatural horror sequences with no combat at all.
prompts.watchFor: Enemies driven by scripted trigger volumes rather than a runtime planner; soldiers who announce a flank and then charge straight ahead; no cover creation by kicking over furniture; squads that fight as individuals with no coordination or suppression; enemies that never retreat; reflex time that slows the player's aim too; firefights with no environmental destruction or particles; horror sequences replaced by more combat.

prompts.title: Battlefield 2
prompts.prompt: Build Battlefield 2 as a multi-file web multiplayer shooter using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), keeping conquest control points, ticket bleed and multi-crew vehicles, and adding the command structure this entry introduced. SQUADS are the unit of play: players group into small squads with a designated SQUAD LEADER, and that leader functions as a mobile SPAWN POINT — so the whole flow of the match becomes keeping a leader alive somewhere useful, and dying no longer means a long run from base. Above them sits one COMMANDER per team, playing a different game entirely from a strategic map view: they see the battlefield, issue orders to squads that appear as objectives on those players' screens, and spend team assets on a cooldown — a UAV that reveals enemies in an area, a satellite scan, an artillery barrage on a marked position, and supply and vehicle drops requested by squad leaders. Commander assets must be destructible on the map, so a team can blind the enemy commander by taking out their radar. Add a persistent rank and unlock progression across matches, six kits with distinct roles including a medic who revives and a support who resupplies ammo, and vehicles from jeeps to jets and helicopters with pilot and gunner seats.
prompts.watchFor: Squads as a chat channel with no spawn-on-leader mechanic; no commander role, or a commander with no assets or no cooldowns; commander assets that cannot be destroyed on the map; squad orders that do not appear as objectives for squad members; kits that differ only in weapon; medics who heal but cannot revive; single-seat aircraft only; no persistent progression between matches.

prompts.title: Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory
prompts.prompt: Build Splinter Cell: Chaos Theory as a multi-file web stealth game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons). Two meters run the game and they must be genuinely simulated, not estimated. The LIGHT meter samples the actual illumination on the player from real light sources, which can be shot out or switched off. The SOUND meter is the subtler one and the acceptance test for this build: it compares the noise the player is MAKING — from movement speed, from the surface material underfoot, from opening a door — against the AMBIENT noise level of the room, so a player can move fast and loudly beside a running generator or in the rain and stay unheard, then must crawl in a silent corridor. Guards need graded perception with investigation, calling for backup and a raised alert state that persists. Build levels with genuinely multiple routes and heavy verticality — pipes, ledges, ziplines, split jumps between two walls, hanging from rails and dropping onto a target — plus interrogations where a grabbed guard is used as a human shield and questioned for intel, a knife for lethal and non-lethal close work, bodies that must be hidden because they will be found, hackable keypads and computers, and an end-of-mission SCORE that rewards ghosting: nobody killed, nobody alerted, nothing left behind.
prompts.watchFor: A vision-cone stealth model with no real light sampling; a sound system that ignores ambient noise, which removes the entire risk-reward of moving fast; guards with a binary alert flag that resets on a timer; bodies that never get discovered; levels with a single stealth path; no vertical traversal; scoring that rewards kills as much as ghosting; interrogation reduced to an instant takedown with no intel.

prompts.title: Guild Wars
prompts.prompt: Build a playable web slice of Guild Wars as a multi-file game, built around the constraint that defines it: the EIGHT-SKILL BAR. The player unlocks hundreds of skills over time but may equip only eight at once, chosen outside combat and locked for the duration of a fight — so the whole depth of the game lives in which eight, how they combine, and how they cover a role, rather than in a growing hotbar. Add a SECONDARY PROFESSION that grants access to a second class's skills at reduced attribute investment, multiplying the combinations, and attribute points spent to scale whole skill lines. Make progression HORIZONTAL: a low level cap reached quickly, gear that tops out at a common maximum so nobody wins by grinding, and everything after that being new skills, builds and cosmetics. Structure the world as instanced: towns and outposts are shared social spaces, but the moment a party leaves into the field they get their OWN private instance of it, so there is no competition for spawns and encounters can be tuned as designed. Let solo players fill their party with hireable henchmen. Build structured PvP as a first-class mode with standardised gear and unlocked skills so matches are decided by build and play, plus co-op missions with bonus objectives.
prompts.watchFor: An unlimited hotbar or more than eight equipped skills, which collapses the entire design; skills swappable mid-combat; a secondary profession that adds stats instead of skill access; vertical gear progression where grinding produces stronger equipment; a shared open world instead of instanced fields; PvP where unlocked gear confers an advantage; no henchmen, forcing group play; attributes that do not scale skill lines.

prompts.title: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion
prompts.prompt: Build The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion as a multi-file web open-world role-playing game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), in a lush, conventional high-fantasy province deliberately unlike its predecessor's alien setting. The headline system is RADIANT AI: every named NPC has a daily schedule and a set of drives, and acts on them — they eat when hungry, sleep at night, go to work, shop, wander to a tavern, hold conversations with EACH OTHER that the player can stand and listen to, react to crimes they witness, and remember the player's reputation. NPCs must be able to fail and improvise, not just walk a fixed patrol. Build the world seamlessly with FAST TRAVEL unlocked only to locations the player has personally discovered on foot, so the map is earned. Include level scaling on encounters and loot — the design decision this entry is genuinely defined by, and the deliberate opposite of the static world in its predecessor — and expose it honestly rather than hiding it. Add the Oblivion gates as hostile planar dungeons that open across the map and can be closed by taking a sigil stone, a persuasion mini-game played on a rotating disc of NPC moods, full guild questlines with their own arcs, spell creation, and a crime and bounty system with guards who will arrest, fine or fight.
prompts.watchFor: NPCs on fixed patrol loops with no schedules, needs or conversations with each other; fast travel available to undiscovered locations from the start; level scaling absent, or applied silently so a player cannot tell; Oblivion gates as ordinary dungeon doors that never open dynamically; persuasion reduced to a single dice roll; guilds as quest lists with no internal politics or ranks; crime with no witnesses, bounty or arrest option.

prompts.title: Company of Heroes
prompts.prompt: Build Company of Heroes as a multi-file web real-time strategy game using three.js (vendored locally, core only — no examples/jsm add-ons), where the battlefield itself is the mechanic. Annotate the terrain with COVER of graded quality — heavy cover behind a stone wall or sandbags, light cover in a hedgerow or crater, and negative cover in open ground where units take extra damage — show it clearly in the UI when ordering a move, and make the difference dramatic enough that a squad in heavy cover beats a larger squad in the open. Then make that cover DESTRUCTIBLE: walls crumble, hedgerows burn, buildings collapse under tank fire, and craters left by shells become new cover, so a long engagement physically erodes and reshapes the terrain it is fought over. Add SUPPRESSION as a separate state from damage — sustained machine-gun fire pins a squad, slowing it to a crawl and eventually forcing it prone until it either retreats or is flanked — making infantry manoeuvre rather than trade shots. Units are SQUADS that lose individual members and are reinforced back to strength in the field. Build the economy from territory: capture points chain back to your base and only connected territory pays out manpower, munitions and fuel, so cutting a supply line strangles an opponent. Give vehicles directional armour so rear and side shots matter.
prompts.watchFor: Cover as a flat damage percentage with no graded types or UI indication; indestructible terrain, which removes the erosion of the battlefield; no suppression, so infantry simply trade damage; individual units instead of reinforceable squads; a global resource trickle rather than territory that must be connected back to base; vehicles with uniform armour on all sides; buildings that cannot be garrisoned or collapsed.

prompts.title: Medieval II: Total War
prompts.prompt: Build Medieval II: Total War as a multi-file web strategy game with both layers — a turn-based campaign map of medieval Europe and North Africa, and real-time 3D battles where MORALE and ROUTING decide the outcome rather than attrition, with contagious routs, flanking, fatigue, charge impact and terrain all feeding morale. On the campaign layer, build the medieval specifics.
